findings.claim: Auditory distraction comes in two kinds (duplex-mechanism account): (a) changing-state interference, where a stream of tokens that differ from one to the next disrupts serial order processing, and (b) attentional diversion, where a deviant or unexpected sound captures attention. In Hughes et al. 2013, only the deviant effect was reduced by top-down factors: harder encoding, a warning in advance and higher working-memory capacity. The changing-state effect was unaffected.
findings.sources: Hughes RW (2014) Auditory distraction: A duplex-mechanism account. PsyCh Journal 3(1):30-41, doi:10.1002/pchj.44. Hughes RW, Hurlstone MJ, Marsh JE, Vachon F, Jones DM (2013) JEP:HPP 39(2):539-553, doi:10.1037/a0029064
findings.design: Review (2014) plus a 3-experiment lab study (2013), visual serial recall with irrelevant sound. Sample sizes not in the abstract.
findings.effect: Deviant effect reduced by encoding difficulty and by a warning in advance. Changing-state effect unaffected by either. WMC predicted the deviant effect, not the changing-state effect. No numeric effect sizes in the abstract.
findings.rule: Treat changing-state content and deviants as separate costs. For verbal jobs, limit how much consecutive tokens differ (fewer distinct tokens, legato rather than staccato); this is a design inference, not a tested parameter. Keep deviants rare and gradual. No number is supported.
findings.engine: Change budget; the Read gate; randomness in hit and note choice (number of distinct tokens)
findings.verification_note: Both citations exist with correct metadata: Crossref for pchj.44 and Europe PMC for a0029064. The 2013 abstract matches the claim. I downgraded the grade from strong to moderate and the replication field to contested, because the duplex account is disputed by unitary and graded-attention accounts (e.g. work from the Buchner/Bell/Röer group, and Halin et al. showing that task difficulty reduces speech disruption in reading). Search budget ran out, so I could not open those counter-papers this session; treat that note as unverified. The rule's 'legato rather than staccato' is an extrapolation.

findings.claim: Fluctuation strength, a psychoacoustic quantity, predicts how much a background sound disrupts verbal short-term memory, using an algorithmic model. (Fluctuation strength is the percept of slow modulation. It peaks at about 4 Hz modulation and gives way to roughness above about 20 Hz; that part is standard psychoacoustics, not this paper.)
findings.sources: Schlittmeier SJ, Weissgerber T, Kerber S, Fastl H, Hellbrück J (2012) Algorithmic modeling of the irrelevant sound effect (ISE) by the hearing sensation fluctuation strength. Attention, Perception & Psychophysics 74(1):194-203, doi:10.3758/s13414-011-0230-7
findings.design: Modelling against pooled behavioural ISE data (70 measurements)
findings.effect: Verified: performance predicted in 63 of 70 cases. Not verified (paywalled): rs = .74, r² = .55, staccato music 0.68 vacil giving +7.5% errors, about 40 sounds. Correction: the abstract says the algorithm overestimated the NON-disturbance of synthetic steady-state sounds (repeated vowel or tone). In other words, it under-predicted their disruption. The researcher's version said the opposite.
findings.rule: Use fluctuation strength (energy in level or pitch modulation around 2-8 Hz, peak 4 Hz) as a proxy for verbal disruption, and keep it low for Read and Write. Do not treat a low-F steady sound as zero cost: the model under-predicts disruption from steady repeated tokens. The 0.68 vacil reference is unverified; do not hard-code it.
findings.engine: Tick and kick density and articulation; modulation rates; tide period; the Read gate
findings.verification_note: Opened the Europe PMC abstract. 63 of 70 is confirmed. The direction of the steady-state misfit was reversed in the finding: the paper says the algorithm 'overestimated the (non-)disturbance impact of synthetic steady-state sounds'. The Spearman, r², vacil and 7.5% figures could not be checked (Springer paywall) and are flagged as unverified.

findings.claim: Neither the changing-state effect nor the auditory deviant effect habituated within a session (8 trials per condition) or across two sessions about a week apart.
findings.sources: Bell R, Mieth L, Röer JP, Troche SJ, Buchner A (2019) Preregistered replication of the auditory deviant effect: A robust benchmark finding. Journal of Cognition 2(1):13, doi:10.5334/joc.64
findings.design: Preregistered lab study, within-subject, N = 273, two sessions 3-24 days apart (mean 7)
findings.effect: Changing-state ηp² = .35 (F(1,272) = 147.80). Deviant ηp² = .10 (F = 30.02). Changing-state × session F = 0.67, p = .41. Deviant × session F = 0.31, p = .58. Condition × trial F(14,259) = 1.44, p = .13. Authors: 'The auditory deviant effect was constant within sessions and across sessions.'
findings.rule: Do not count on users habituating to changing-state content or deviants within a session or across days. No number is supported for a habituation time.
findings.engine: The Read gate; randomness in note and hit choice; pattern vocabulary
findings.verification_note: Opened the full text on journalofcognition.org. Every statistic matches. I added the paper's title, which the finding left out. I raised the grade to strong: the study is preregistered with a large N. The replication field stays 'contested' because earlier Röer et al. work reported habituation of the deviant effect.

findings.claim: Acoustic and categorical deviation effects come from different mechanisms. The two effects were additive, and only the acoustic deviation effect habituated (declined over the session).
findings.sources: Littlefair Z, Vachon F, Ball LJ, Robinson N, Marsh JE (2022) Acoustic, and categorical, deviation effects are produced by different mechanisms: evidence from additivity and habituation. Auditory Perception & Cognition 5(1-2):1-24, doi:10.1080/25742442.2022.2063609
findings.design: Two online experiments. Ns (192, 188) and the 6-of-54 deviant schedule are as reported by the researcher; I could not verify them.
findings.effect: Direction only: additive effects; habituation for acoustic deviation only (second summary in the Bell 2019 search results). No effect sizes verified.
findings.rule: If an occasional change must exist, prefer a purely acoustic variant (timbre, register, texture) over a new recognisable object or category. Do not rely on a specific number of repeats for fading.
findings.engine: Change budget; what kind of element may change
findings.verification_note: Crossref confirms title, authors, venue, volume and pages. Tandfonline returned 403, so I could not open the abstract. The 'only acoustic habituates' result was corroborated by a search-result summary ('habituation was only observed for the acoustic deviation effect'). The Ns, the trial schedule and 'about 3 exposures' are unverified, so I removed them from the effect field.

findings.claim: Auditory capture comes from violating a learned expectation, not from novelty. With a voice change every 5 trials, capture appeared only after the expectation formed, weakened as the changes became predictable, and returned when the pattern was violated.
findings.sources: Vachon F, Hughes RW, Jones DM (2012) Broken expectations: Violation of expectancies, not novelty, captures auditory attention. JEP:LMC 38(1):164-177, doi:10.1037/a0025054
findings.design: Lab, visual serial recall with irrelevant speech; Ns not retrieved
findings.effect: Direction only, as stated in the abstract
findings.rule: A change on a learnable schedule loses its capture value, and breaking the schedule restores it. Either keep the change cadence regular or make changes too gradual to register as events. No number is supported.
findings.engine: Section length regularity; tide period; change budget scheduling
findings.verification_note: The Europe PMC abstract matches every element of the claim. 'Replicated' is reasonable because Parmentier 2014 (C1-06) reviews converging prediction-violation evidence, though no direct replication was checked.

findings.claim: Review: deviant distraction is the time cost of involuntary orienting to the deviant and back. It is driven by violation of the system's predictions, not by rarity. Memory load and cognitive control reduce it; ageing and induced emotion increase it.
findings.sources: Parmentier FBR (2014) The cognitive determinants of behavioral distraction by deviant auditory stimuli: a review. Psychological Research 78(3):321-338, doi:10.1007/s00426-013-0534-4
findings.design: Narrative review
findings.effect: No pooled effect size
findings.rule: Distraction scales with prediction error, not rarity. An unpredicted abrupt event costs time; a slow, expected change costs little. No number is supported.
findings.engine: Change budget; fade lengths
findings.verification_note: The Europe PMC abstract matches every point: prediction violation not rarity, orienting time cost, memory load and control reduce it, ageing and emotion increase it. The abstract also says behavioural distraction is not just a by-product of MMN, P3a or RON.

findings.claim: Pitch deviants of 1-10% in the tones being judged slow responses and elicit ERP distraction markers, and both effects grow with deviance size. At 1%, trials with slowed reaction times showed stronger later ERP responses, while early change detection looked similar. Separately, N1/MMN, P3a and RON are not a tightly coupled chain.
findings.sources: Berti S, Roeber U, Schröger E (2004) Experimental Psychology 51(4):249-257, doi:10.1027/1618-3169.51.4.249. Horváth J, Winkler I, Bendixen A (2008) Biological Psychology 79(2):139-147, doi:10.1016/j.biopsycho.2008.04.001
findings.design: Lab ERP studies; Berti N = 20, duration judgement of tones with occasional pitch deviants
findings.effect: Behavioural and ERP distraction increase with deviance from 1% to 10%. Millisecond values not verified; the '>35 ms' figure is unverified.
findings.task: Duration judgement where the pitch change is an irrelevant feature of the attended tone
findings.rule: Abrupt pitch steps as small as 1% can cost something, and the cost grows with step size. Prefer glides and crossfades for pitch or level changes in held layers. Caveat: the deviant was a feature of the tone being judged, not a background layer, so the 1% threshold may not transfer to unattended beds.
findings.engine: Fade lengths; glide and crossfade on retunes; note choice for held voices
findings.verification_note: Both papers exist with correct metadata (Crossref for Berti; Europe PMC for Horváth, where I added the DOI and issue). The abstracts support the direction and the dissociation. I downgraded the grade to moderate: the rule generalises from task-relevant tones to a background layer, and no millisecond costs were verified.

findings.claim: Slow change deafness: when continuous speech gradually shifted in pitch by 3 semitones, nearly 50% of listeners failed to notice, although the change was above threshold. Alerting listeners greatly improved detection, and larger changes reduced misses.
findings.sources: Neuhoff JG, Wayand J, Ndiaye MC, Berkow AB, Bertacchi BR, Benton CA (2015) Slow change deafness. Attention, Perception & Psychophysics 77(4):1189-1199, doi:10.3758/s13414-015-0871-z
findings.design: Lab experiments; Ns and ramp duration not retrieved
findings.effect: About 50% miss rate for a 3-semitone gradual shift (Exp 1); alerting improved detection; larger changes gave less deafness
findings.rule: Slow, continuous drift can go unnoticed by about half of listeners who are not expecting it, at least up to 3 semitones (ramp rate unknown). Telling users the sound evolves will increase noticing. No safe rate is supported.
findings.engine: Fade lengths; tide period; change size; onboarding copy
findings.verification_note: Europe PMC abstract: 'nearly 50% failed to notice the change'. Alerting and change-size effects are confirmed. The ramp duration is still unknown.

findings.claim: Listeners overestimate rising-level change relative to an equal falling change, and the asymmetry grows with level. A 2026 study shows that a time-varying loudness model predicts this asymmetry, so an adaptive 'looming' bias is not needed to explain it.
findings.sources: Neuhoff JG (1998) Perceptual bias for rising tones. Nature 395:123-124, doi:10.1038/25862. Kolarik AJ, Koblitz A, Moore BCJ, van der Linde I, Campbell W, Pardhan S (2026) A loudness model for time-varying sounds predicts asymmetries in estimates of loudness change for sounds that increase or decrease in level. Hearing Research 481 (UEA repository 104257)
findings.design: Lab psychophysics
findings.effect: Rising > falling perceived change, larger at higher levels; magnitude not retrieved
findings.rule: For the same level change, make fade-ins slower or shallower than fade-outs, especially at higher levels. No ratio is supported.
findings.engine: Asymmetric fade-in vs fade-out; Sensory Guard ceilings
findings.verification_note: Crossref confirms Neuhoff 1998. The Kolarik item is not just a preprint: the UEA record says it is published in Hearing Research vol. 481 (2026). I corrected the citation and author list. That record confirms the asymmetry grows with level and is predicted by the loudness model.

findings.claim: Consensus characteristics of habituation: more frequent stimulation habituates faster and/or more strongly; weaker stimuli habituate faster; withheld stimuli show spontaneous recovery; a different stimulus dishabituates; dishabituation itself habituates; habituation is somewhat stimulus-specific; long-term habituation exists.
findings.sources: Rankin CH, Abrams T, Barry RJ, Bhatnagar S, Clayton DF, Colombo J, Coppola G, Geyer MA, Glanzman DL, Marsland S, McSweeney FK, Wilson DA, Wu CF, Thompson RF (2009) Neurobiology of Learning and Memory 92(2):135-138, doi:10.1016/j.nlm.2008.09.012
findings.design: Consensus review
findings.effect: Qualitative
findings.rule: Quiet, frequently recurring elements fade from notice fastest. Elements absent for a long time regain salience when they return. A new element can re-awaken response to the old ones. The claim that 'each change spends attention twice' is an inference, not from the paper. No numbers are supported.
findings.engine: Change budget; element dropout and re-entry; level of recurring elements
findings.verification_note: Read PMC2754195 and matched characteristics #2, #4, #5, #7, #8, #9 and #10 by their wording. Sub-points such as 'very intense stimuli may not habituate', 'recovery is faster after frequent stimulation' and 'hours to weeks' were not individually quoted. The 'spends attention twice' line in the rule is flagged as interpretation.

findings.claim: Lab: disruption from speech and from office noise habituated with exposure, with partial dishabituation after a quiet period. Field: 88 office workers reported no habituation to office noise.
findings.sources: Banbury S, Berry DC (1997) Habituation and dishabituation to speech and office noise. JEP: Applied 3(3):181-195, doi:10.1037/1076-898X.3.3.181. Banbury SP, Berry DC (2005) Office noise and employee concentration: identifying causes of disruption and potential improvements. Ergonomics 48(1):25-37
findings.design: Lab experiments (1997); field questionnaire survey, N = 88 at two sites (2005)
findings.effect: Field: 99% reported that noise impaired concentration; 'no evidence for habituation' (self-report). Lab: the 20-minute habituation and 5-minute quiet figures are unverified (abstract not accessible).
findings.rule: Keep the bed continuous through a session and avoid long silent gaps. Do not plan on a 20-minute habituation: it is unverified, and the field study and Bell 2019 (C1-03) found none.
findings.engine: Section length; gaps between sections; session-start fades
findings.verification_note: Crossref confirms the 1997 citation, but its abstract could not be opened (PsycNet loads dynamically and the Reading repository blocked the request). I verified and completed the 2005 field citation via Europe PMC: Ergonomics 48(1):25-37, a self-report survey. I downgraded the grade to weak because the 20-minute and 5-minute figures could not be checked.

findings.claim: Listeners rapidly and without supervision form memories for arbitrary noise samples that recur. Performance jumps abruptly to near-perfect, and several noises were remembered weeks later. The same was later shown for random click (time) patterns.
findings.sources: Agus TR, Thorpe SJ, Pressnitzer D (2010) Rapid formation of robust auditory memories: insights from noise. Neuron 66(4):610-618, doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2010.04.014. Kang H, Agus TR, Pressnitzer D (2017) Auditory memory for random time patterns. JASA 142(4):2219, doi:10.1121/1.5007730
findings.design: Lab psychophysics with active repetition detection in noise
findings.effect: Abrupt learning to near-perfect; retention over 'several weeks'. The press figures (about 2 hearings trained, about 10 naive) are unverified: the ScienceDaily page returned 404.
findings.rule: Do not loop a frozen noise or texture buffer: identical recurring noise is learnable and remembered across sessions. Generate noise procedurally or re-randomise it. The exposure count needed during passive background listening is unknown.
findings.engine: Noise and texture generation; tuned-noise voice; air layers
findings.verification_note: Europe PMC confirms the Neuron abstract ('abruptly near-perfect', 'several weeks'). I added the full Kang 2017 citation. The 2-vs-10 exposure figures came from a press summary I could not open, so I removed them from the rule.

findings.claim: Recycled frozen noise is heard as a global repetition percept for periods up to about 1 s. With extended listening, brief recurring features (clicks, thumps) are noticed. With a cross-modal cuing method, listeners could detect repeats of waveform portions recurring after 10 s or more.
findings.sources: Warren RM, Bashford JA Jr, Cooley JM, Brubaker BS (2001) Detection of acoustic repetition for very long stochastic patterns. Perception & Psychophysics 63(1):175-182, doi:10.3758/BF03200511
findings.design: Lab; Exp 1 used cross-modal cuing with long-period frozen noise; Exp 2 compared spectral bands
findings.effect: Repetition of 10 s or more is detectable with cuing; the 6-kHz band is especially difficult. Not verified: 13 repetitions, 0.4% tap error, 45 naive listeners tapping at 10 s periods.
findings.task: Detecting and tapping to repeated noise
findings.rule: Loops of 1 s or less are plainly audible as loops, and periods of 10 s or more are still detectable under favourable listening. Avoid exact repetition of noise textures at any practical period; prefer non-repeating generation.
findings.engine: Loop lengths of noise or sampled layers; texture generation
findings.verification_note: The Europe PMC abstract confirms the citation, the global percept up to 1 s, the clicks and thumps, and 10 s+ detection with cross-modal cuing. It does not confirm the '2 s with difficulty' or '13 cycles' figures, or uncued naive tapping. Those are unverified, so I removed them. Changed the replication field to single study.

findings.claim: The brain detects the emergence of a repeating tone pattern in a random stream almost as fast as an ideal observer. This happens in naive listeners attending a visual task (MEG). Behaviourally, a transition back to randomness is detected within about 3 tones.
findings.sources: Barascud N, Pearce MT, Griffiths TD, Friston KJ, Chait M (2016) PNAS 113(5):E616-E625, doi:10.1073/pnas.1508523113 (PMC4747708)
findings.design: Behaviour N = 11 (active); MEG N = 13 and 13 (naive, visual N-back); fMRI N = 16 (passive)
findings.effect: 10-tone cycles: 773 ms (15.5 tones), 88.5% within 2 cycles. 20-tone cycles: 1682 ms, 80.4% within 2 cycles. Regular to random: 155 ms (about 3 tones) for 10-tone cycles and 415 ms for 20-tone cycles. Ideal observer: 1 cycle + 4 tones (Exp 1), 1 cycle + 3 tones (Exp 4).
findings.rule: Exact repeating figures are registered within about 1-2 cycles without attention, and a break is registered within a few events. Each break is a prediction error.
findings.engine: Pattern variation rate; break rate; pattern vocabulary
findings.verification_note: Read the PMC full text. All numbers match except the regular-to-random range: it is 155 ms (10-tone) and 415 ms (20-tone), not 155-281 ms. Fixed in the effect field.

findings.claim: Predictability is not salient: regular tone patterns did not capture attention in two behavioural tasks, although EEG responses to regular sequences rose relative to random ones.
findings.sources: Southwell R, Baumann A, Gal C, Barascud N, Friston K, Chait M (2017) Is predictability salient? A study of attentional capture by auditory patterns. Phil Trans R Soc B 372(1714):20160105, doi:10.1098/rstb.2016.0105
findings.design: Lab EEG plus two behavioural experiments
findings.effect: Larger neural response to regular sequences; authors conclude 'regularity does not capture attention'
findings.task: Behavioural capture tasks with tone sequences
findings.rule: Making a figure regular does not by itself make it attention-grabbing. That variation should be budgeted for boredom rather than salience is an inference.
findings.engine: Randomness in note and hit choice; pattern variation rate
findings.verification_note: Europe PMC abstract and Crossref (vol. 372, issue 1714) checked. The claim matches.

findings.claim: Tone patterns that reoccur about every 3 minutes inside random streams become implicitly remembered. A reaction-time advantage emerged by block 2 (after about 6 reoccurrences) and was retained at 24 hours and 7 weeks, without correlating with explicit familiarity.
findings.sources: Bianco R, Harrison PMC, Hu M, Bolger C, Picken S, Pearce MT, Chait M (2020) Long-term implicit memory for sequential auditory patterns in humans. eLife 9:e56073, doi:10.7554/eLife.56073
findings.design: Lab: pilot plus 7 experiments (N = 18-30 each; pooled N = 147). 1 s patterns (20 × 50 ms tones), 3 per 8-minute block, 9-15 reoccurrences per session.
findings.effect: Exp 1A: about 140 ms in block 2 (t(18) = 3.96, p = .006), plateau at 233 ms. 24 h vs 7 weeks: t(13) = -0.668, p = .515. Explicit familiarity was above chance but did not correlate with the RT advantage.
findings.task: Active detection of regular patterns in random tone streams
findings.rule: Fixed figures that recur every few minutes are likely to become implicitly familiar within a session and to persist across weeks. Caveat: this was shown with active detection of 1 s patterns, not with background music during work.
findings.engine: Pattern vocabulary size; across-session variation; per-session seed
findings.verification_note: Read the eLife full text. All numbers match except the pilot ηp² values, which I did not see. I corrected 'did not depend on explicit recognition': explicit familiarity was above chance but uncorrelated with the RT advantage. I softened the rule's claim that users will know the figures by the second session, since the task was active rather than background.

findings.claim: Adults and infants segment continuous tone streams into 'tone words' using transitional probabilities, as they do with syllables. Statistical learning is not specific to language.
findings.sources: Saffran JR, Johnson EK, Aslin RN, Newport EL (1999) Statistical learning of tone sequences by human infants and adults. Cognition 70(1):27-52, doi:10.1016/S0010-0277(98)00075-4
findings.design: Lab: passive exposure, then familiarity test; exposure duration not verified
findings.effect: Above-chance segmentation comparable to syllables (not numerically verified)
findings.task: Passive listening, then forced-choice familiarity test
findings.rule: Consistent transition rules in note choice are learnable passively, so a rule-based generator becomes 'familiar but not looped'. No exposure time is supported.
findings.engine: Transition-matrix design for note choice
findings.verification_note: Crossref confirms the citation. Europe PMC had no record and ScienceDirect returned 403, so I could not read the abstract or check the infant age. I downgraded the grade to moderate because the content was not verified in this session, though the finding is widely known.

findings.claim: Musical expectation is well modelled as probabilistic prediction from statistically learned variable-order Markov models (IDyOM), which give per-event information content and entropy.
findings.sources: Pearce MT (2018) Statistical learning and probabilistic prediction in music cognition: mechanisms of stylistic enculturation. Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences 1423(1):378-395, doi:10.1111/nyas.13654
findings.design: Review of IDyOM simulations
findings.effect: No single effect size
findings.rule: Quantify generator predictability as IC and entropy and set targets per job. No absolute IC target is supported for background use.
findings.engine: Note and hit randomness quantified as IC and entropy
findings.verification_note: The Europe PMC abstract confirms the title, the IDyOM review and its scope (expectation, emotion, memory, segmentation, meter). I did not separately check volume and pages.

findings.claim: Liking for music is an inverted-U function of both mean information content and entropy. Study 1 showed a marginal IC × entropy interaction (p = .06), with low-IC music preferred more strongly when entropy was high.
findings.sources: Gold BP, Pearce MT, Mas-Herrero E, Dagher A, Zatorre RJ (2019) Predictability and uncertainty in the pleasure of music: a reward for learning? Journal of Neuroscience 39(47):9397-9409, doi:10.1523/JNEUROSCI.0428-19.2019 (PMC6867811)
findings.design: Study 1 N = 43, 55 excerpts; Study 2 N = 27, 12 excerpts × 7 presentations
findings.effect: IC quadratic β = -0.09 and -0.18; entropy quadratic β = -0.06 (p = .003) and -0.25; variance explained 26.3/41.6% (IC) and 19.1/34.9% (entropy). Study 1 also had a negative linear IC term (β = -0.21). Interaction p = .06, ηp² = .07 (Study 1 only).
findings.rule: Set note-generator surprise and uncertainty at or a little below the corpus average, not at the extremes. The peak positions are derived by the researcher, not reported in the paper, and the paper measured attentive liking, not background suitability.
findings.engine: IC and entropy targets per state
findings.verification_note: Read the PMC full text. The coefficients match. I corrected the claim that predictable continuations were preferred more under high uncertainty: that interaction was marginal (p = .06) and tested only in Study 1. Changed the replication field to single study (two studies in one paper).

findings.claim: Uncertainty and surprise jointly predict musical pleasure. Chords were rated most pleasurable when they were surprising in a low-uncertainty context, or unsurprising in a high-uncertainty context. The nucleus accumbens reflected only uncertainty.
findings.sources: Cheung VKM, Harrison PMC, Meyer L, Pearce MT, Haynes J-D, Koelsch S (2019) Current Biology 29(23):4084-4092.e4, doi:10.1016/j.cub.2019.09.067
findings.design: Model-based analysis of about 80,000 chords from Billboard songs, with behavioural ratings and fMRI
findings.effect: Significant uncertainty × surprise interaction; coefficients not retrieved
findings.rule: Avoid the 'low uncertainty plus high surprise' combination that maximises pleasure and draws attention in background audio. Keep harmonic surprise low in predictable contexts. No number is supported.
findings.engine: Chord and note randomness; the four-part crossfade voice
findings.verification_note: The Europe PMC abstract confirms the claim. I changed the replication field from 'replicated' to 'single study', since no independent replication was checked.

findings.claim: Of 57 music-preference studies over 115 years, 50 (87.7%) were compatible with a segmented inverted-U relation, 5 (8.8%) were mixed and 2 (3.5%) were incompatible.
findings.sources: Chmiel A, Schubert E (2017) Back to the inverted-U for music preference: A review of the literature. Psychology of Music 45(6):886-909, doi:10.1177/0305735617697507
findings.design: Categorical review of 57 studies
findings.effect: 50/57 compatible; 5 mixed; 2 incompatible
findings.rule: The change budget has an optimum, not a 'less is always better' direction. No peak location for background listening is supported.
findings.engine: Change budget; pattern variation
findings.verification_note: The Crossref abstract confirms all the counts. I added the 5 mixed studies.

findings.claim: Mere-exposure meta-analysis: repeated exposure gives an inverted-U for liking (positive linear, negative quadratic), but the inverted-U appeared only for visual stimuli, not auditory ones. It also appeared only for exposures under 10 s or over 1 minute. Bornstein's 1989 meta-analysis gave r = .26.
findings.sources: Montoya RM, Horton RS, Vevea JL, Citkowicz M, Lauber EA (2017) Psychological Bulletin 143(5):459-498, doi:10.1037/bul0000085. Bornstein RF (1989) Psychological Bulletin 106(2):265-289
findings.design: Meta-analysis of 268 curve estimates from 81 articles
findings.effect: Inverted U overall; inverted-U moderation: visual yes, auditory no
findings.rule: Do not rely on mere exposure to make the bed better liked over sessions. The meta-analysis did not find the exposure-liking curve for auditory stimuli. No auditory number is supported.
findings.engine: Pattern vocabulary; across-session variation
findings.verification_note: The Europe PMC abstract confirms the 268/81 counts, the curve shape and that 'inverted-U curves appeared only for visual stimuli, not auditory'. The original 'null for auditory' overstated this: the abstract speaks to the curve shape. Bornstein r = .26 was not verified this session.

findings.claim: Listening mode matters. With incidental listening, liking increased with more exposures, more so for ecologically valid music. With focused listening to the most realistic music, liking rose and then fell (inverted U).
findings.sources: Szpunar KK, Schellenberg EG, Pliner P (2004) Liking and memory for musical stimuli as a function of exposure. JEP:LMC 30(2):370-381, doi:10.1037/0278-7393.30.2.370
findings.design: Lab, 3 experiments; exposure counts and Ns not verified
findings.effect: Direction confirmed from the abstract. Not verified: 2/8/32 and 4/16/64 exposures, F and t values, N = 50/40/60.
findings.task: Focused vs incidental exposure, then liking and recognition ratings
findings.rule: Material that stays in the background tolerates (and may benefit from) repetition, while attended repetition leads to satiation. Spend the change budget on keeping attention off the music. Specific repetition counts are unverified.
findings.engine: Pattern variation rate; vocabulary size; change budget
findings.verification_note: The Europe PMC abstract confirms the direction for incidental (monotonic increase) and focused (inverted U for realistic music). None of the numeric details could be verified, so the rule's '32-64' and '8 attended repetitions' are flagged.

findings.claim: The vigilance sensitivity decrement is moderated by task type (larger for high event rates and successive discrimination). Vigilance is resource-demanding and stressful, which supports resource theory over mindlessness accounts. That much of the decline occurs in the first 15 minutes is a classic claim, attributed to Teichner 1974 and not verified here.
findings.sources: See JE, Howe SR, Warm JS, Dember WN (1995) Meta-analysis of the sensitivity decrement in vigilance. Psychological Bulletin 117(2):230-249, doi:10.1037/0033-2909.117.2.230. Warm JS, Parasuraman R, Matthews G (2008) Human Factors 50(3):433-441, doi:10.1518/001872008X312152. Teichner WH (1974), cited second-hand.
findings.design: Meta-analysis plus review
findings.effect: Pooled d values not retrieved. The 15-minute and 10-15% Mackworth figures are second-hand and unverified.
findings.rule: Alertness loss on monotonous monitoring is front-loaded, plausibly within the first 15-30 minutes, so any alerting drift is more useful early than at a fixed 90 minutes. Treat the timing as approximate. No evidence was found that background sound reverses the decrement.
findings.engine: Section length; timing of state changes; tide period
findings.verification_note: Crossref confirms See 1995 (abstract not available). Europe PMC confirms the Warm 2008 abstract (resource theory, workload, stress). The timing figures rest on secondary citations I could not open, so I downgraded the grade from strong to moderate.

findings.claim: The claim that brief, rare mental breaks prevent the vigilance decrement (goal-habituation) did not hold in a large test. In N = 498, brief task switches and content-free cues did not reduce the decrement, and Bayesian analyses favoured the null.
findings.sources: Ariga A, Lleras A (2011) Cognition 118(3):439-443, doi:10.1016/j.cognition.2010.12.007. Helton WS, Russell PN (2012) Experimental Brain Research 219(1):37-46, doi:10.1007/s00221-012-3065-0
findings.design: Original lab study (digit memory with intermittent recall) vs large test (N = 498)
findings.effect: Original: the decrement was prevented when digits were recalled intermittently. Helton: equivalent decrement in all groups (sensitivity and RT); 'substantial evidence in favour of the null'.
findings.rule: Do not insert periodic sonic 'refresh' cues to reset attention. Content-free cues did not help, and they would spend the change budget on deviants. No number is supported.
findings.engine: Change budget; section boundaries
findings.verification_note: Both abstracts were read on Europe PMC. The Ariga N = 84 was not verified. Helton was not a strict direct replication (it used different manipulations), but it tested the same theory.

findings.claim: Preferred background music increased task-focus and reduced mind-wandering on a psychomotor vigilance task, without changing external distraction (lab). Online, music beat both silence and noise, and also gave slightly faster reaction times. Mood and arousal mediated the effects, and faster tempo was linked to more mind-wandering in one experiment.
findings.sources: Kiss L, Linnell KJ (2021) Psychological Research 85(6):2313-2325, doi:10.1007/s00426-020-01400-6. Kiss L, Linnell KJ (2024) The role of mood and arousal in the effect of background music on attentional state and performance during a sustained attention task. Scientific Reports 14:9485, doi:10.1038/s41598-024-60218-z
findings.design: Lab within-subject N = 40 (2021); online N = 106 (vs silence) and N = 77 (vs noise), about 25 minutes per condition (2024)
findings.effect: 2024: task-focus b = -0.181 (p = .005) and -0.382 (p < .001); mind-wandering b = 0.437 and 0.741 (p < .001); RT faster with music (p = .047, p = .030; about 8 ms). Tempo linked to mind-wandering in Exp 2 only (p = .004). 2021: no significant RT benefit.
findings.population: Students and online adults who habitually listen to music while working; self-selected music
findings.rule: For low-demand sustained work (Hours or Hold), continuous music can reduce mind-wandering, probably via mood and arousal, so silence is not the neutral optimum. The evidence used preferred music in habitual music-listeners. Time on task was only a covariate, so no section-length number is supported.
findings.engine: Hours and Hold design; Character dial; tempo per job
findings.verification_note: Read the 2024 PMC full text and the 2021 abstract. The b values and the tempo result match. Correction: the 2024 online studies did find faster RTs with music, and the original finding omitted this. I added the sample's self-selection (habitual music-listeners). Thomson et al. 2014 was not checked and was dropped.

findings.claim: Background-music meta-analysis: no overall effect of music vs no music, because specific effects cancel. Music impairs reading, slightly hurts memory, and improves emotional reactions and sports performance. Music tempo influences the tempo of concurrent activity.
findings.sources: Kämpfe J, Sedlmeier P, Renkewitz F (2011) The impact of background music on adult listeners: A meta-analysis. Psychology of Music 39(4):424-448, doi:10.1177/0305735610376261
findings.design: Meta-analysis
findings.effect: Directions confirmed. Not verified: r = .03 global, reading -.11, memory -.09, tempo r = .40, year r = .01.
findings.rule: Expect small effects overall, negative for reading and memory. For Read and Write, the engine should cost as little as possible. Tempo carryover to behaviour supports tempo per job as a lever.
findings.engine: Tempo per job; the Read gate
findings.verification_note: Crossref confirms the citation and the abstract's directions. The numeric r values and the 'no decline with publication year' claim could not be checked, so they are flagged as unverified.

findings.claim: Popular claim: attention lasts only about 10 minutes (or 8 seconds). An editorial review finds the 10-15 minute lecture-attention limit rests on repeated citation, not primary evidence. The most-cited source barely discusses attention, and teacher differences explain most of the variation.
findings.sources: Bradbury NA (2016) Attention span during lectures: 8 seconds, 10 minutes, or more? Advances in Physiology Education 40(4):509-513, doi:10.1152/advan.00109.2016
findings.design: Critical review / editorial
findings.effect: No reliable evidence for a fixed span
findings.rule: Do not set section length to a '10-minute attention reset'. No fixed span is supported.
findings.engine: Section length; change budget
findings.verification_note: The Europe PMC abstract matches. The article is an editorial. The 'false' grade refers to the popular claim.

findings.claim: Popular claim: a waking 90-minute basic rest-activity cycle means focus sessions should run in 90-minute cycles. The REM cycle was shown to be sleep-dependent, and waking ultradian performance rhythms are weak and inconsistent.
findings.sources: Moses J, Lubin A, Johnson LC, Naitoh P (1977) Rapid eye movement cycle is a sleep-dependent rhythm. Nature 265:360-361, doi:10.1038/265360a0. LaJambe CM, Brown FM (2008) Ultradian cognitive performance rhythms during sleep deprivation. In Ultradian Rhythms from Molecules to Mind, Springer, pp. 283-301, doi:10.1007/978-1-4020-8352-5_13
findings.design: Lab (1977); book chapter (2008)
findings.effect: No confirmed common BRAC
findings.task: Performance and arousal across the day
findings.rule: Do not anchor tide or session length to 90 minutes on biological grounds.
findings.engine: Tide period; session length
findings.verification_note: Crossref confirms both citations, and I added the chapter pages. The Moses title states the claim directly. The chapter's content was not opened, so the characterisation of waking rhythms is unverified beyond the title.

findings.claim: Melodies driven by 1/f noise sounded pleasing, white-noise melodies too random and 1/f² melodies too correlated. This was an informal impression. The measured result is that power and frequency fluctuations in music, and power fluctuations in speech, follow approximately 1/f spectra.
findings.sources: Voss RF, Clarke J (1978) '1/f noise' in music: Music from 1/f noise. JASA 63(1):258-263, doi:10.1121/1.381721
findings.design: Spectral analysis plus informal listening
findings.effect: Qualitative listening comparison
findings.rule: Consider 1/f processes for slow drifts as a starting point, not an evidenced optimum.
findings.engine: Note and hit randomness; tide shape
findings.verification_note: The Crossref abstract matches. Nuance: speech frequency fluctuations are not 1/f; they have a characteristic time of about 0.1 s.

findings.claim: Eno on Music for Airports: loops repeat every 23.5 s, about 25 7/8 s and about 29 15/16 s, in 'incommensurable' cycles that are 'not likely to come back into sync again'.
findings.sources: Eno B (1996) 'Generative Music', talk at the Imagination Conference, San Francisco, 8 June 1996; transcript at In Motion Magazine, https://inmotionmagazine.com/eno1.html
findings.design: Practitioner account
findings.effect: No measured effect
findings.rule: Give recurring layers mutually incommensurate periods, each well above 10-20 s, so the combined texture does not recur.
findings.engine: Loop and phrase periods per voice; tide periods
findings.verification_note: Opened the transcript. The quotes match ('23 1/2', '25 7/8 ... or something like that', '29 15/16 ... or something'). 29 15/16 s = 29.94 s.

findings.claim: Game-audio practice: excessive repetition in game music is described as contributing to listener fatigue, lower enjoyment and weaker immersion. Expressive variation was less noticeable during gameplay than in isolated listening, but it still affected perceived repetition.
findings.sources: Worrall K (2025) Expressive Performance Rendering for Reduced Music Repetition in Video Games. PhD thesis, University of York, https://etheses.whiterose.ac.uk/38684/
findings.design: Doctoral thesis with an in-game study
findings.effect: Qualitative; no effect sizes
findings.rule: Variation is less noticeable when the listener is busy, so subtle variation suffices during focused work. A no-repeat window in variant pools is reasonable practice, but no N is evidenced.
findings.engine: No-repeat window; vocabulary size
findings.verification_note: The Worrall thesis was opened and confirmed. The Dutta (Huddersfield) thesis could not be located (404) and the Audiokinetic Q&A returned 403. I removed both, along with the '15 variants, avoid last 10' figure.

findings.claim: Huron's ITPRA theory: expectation-related feelings arise from Imagination, Tension, Prediction, Reaction and Appraisal responses. Accurate prediction is rewarded, and fast reaction responses are defensive reflexes to sudden events.
findings.sources: Huron D (2006) Sweet Anticipation: Music and the Psychology of Expectation. MIT Press
findings.design: Theoretical monograph
findings.effect: No effect size
findings.rule: Favour predictable continuations and avoid sudden onsets. No number is supported.
findings.engine: Note and hit randomness; onset ramps
findings.verification_note: The MIT Press page returned 403 and the ISBN lookup in Crossref was empty. The book and the ITPRA framework are well established, but I did not open the source this session; the ISBN is unverified.

findings.claim: In natural scenes, bottom-up salience is driven most by a rise in loudness, then by rises in harmonicity, brightness and pitch. Salience depends on context: a loud event draws less response when loudness also rose in the preceding seconds, and a repeated sound loses salience.
findings.sources: Huang N, Elhilali M (2017). Auditory salience using natural soundscapes. J Acoust Soc Am 141(3):2163-2176. PMC6909985. Online replication: Kothinti SR, Huang N, Elhilali M (2021). Auditory salience using natural scenes: an online study. J Acoust Soc Am 150(4):2952-2966. doi:10.1121/10.0006750
findings.design: Lab study, N=50 (ages 18-34). Continuous dichotic report across 20 natural scenes, plus 14 passive pupil-only listeners. Online replication with a crowdsourced sample.
findings.effect: Before salient events: loudness t(232)=11.6, harmonicity t=7.3, brightness t=4.0, pitch t=3.0, and the 'scale' (bandwidth) feature decreased (t=-3.8). Loudness alone hit about 66% of events (82% in sparse scenes, 58% in dense ones); harmonicity alone 59%. A loudness rise in the preceding 0-8 s window weakened the response, t(381)=2.68, p=.0077. No standardised effect sizes.
findings.task: Passive listening with continuous salience report (no concurrent cognitive task)
findings.rule: The largest pop-out lever is an element's loudness step relative to the preceding few seconds. Loudness dominates more in sparse scenes, so in a sparse bed the size of the level step decides salience. Repeated, familiar elements are cheaper than novel ones. A rise in harmonicity or brightness at entry adds salience. No dB threshold is supported.
findings.engine: Element fade-ins (entry level vs. bed), bed density/voicing, Sensory Guard (feature-change detector)
findings.verification_note: I opened PMC6909985. N=50, 14 pupil listeners, 20 scenes, and every t-value and percentage match the paper. Correction: the paper reports 'scale' (its bandwidth measure) as DECREASING before events (t=-3.8). The finding's wording 'broader spectral scale was more salient' is an interpretation whose direction I could not confirm, so I removed it. I confirmed the Kothinti 2021 citation via Crossref: its abstract says online data match lab results. The same abstract also says low-level features 'do not fully explain' natural-scene salience. I did not locate the repeated-knock detail in what I read.

findings.claim: Saliency-map models (Kayser-style, built on the visual saliency map) predict human salience in natural sound scenes only weakly. Models of feature change against the background statistics do better.
findings.sources: Kayser C, Petkov CI, Lippert M, Logothetis NK (2005). Mechanisms for allocating auditory attention: an auditory saliency map. Curr Biol 15(21):1943-1947. doi:10.1016/j.cub.2005.09.040. Benchmark: Huang & Elhilali (2017) JASA 141(3):2163, PMC6909985.
findings.design: Kayser: computational model validated on human and macaque saliency judgements. Huang & Elhilali: benchmark against continuous human salience reports (N=50).
findings.effect: AUC for predicting human salient events: Kayser about 0.58, Kim about 0.65, Kaya about 0.71, Huang & Elhilali feature-change LDA about 0.74.
findings.task: Salience judgement or detection in natural scenes
findings.rule: A Sensory Guard should not rely on an image-style saliency map. A detector of change against recent statistics (loudness, harmonicity, centroid, pitch, bandwidth) works better, but it reaches only about AUC 0.74 on natural scenes, so treat it as a screen, not proof of safety.
findings.engine: Sensory Guard (salience check)
findings.verification_note: I confirmed the AUC values in PMC6909985. The Kayser 2005 citation is correct (well-established). Correction: the AUC comparison comes from one benchmark by the developers of the winning model, so I changed replication to 'single study'. Kothinti 2021 supports the broader point that low-level features under-explain salience. The grade stays moderate.

findings.claim: The brain flags as salient any deviation from the running background statistics, in a multidimensional feature space (pitch, intensity, timbre and others). This is consistent with, and proposed as, a predictive-coding account.
findings.sources: Kaya EM, Elhilali M (2014). Investigating bottom-up auditory attention. Front Hum Neurosci 8:327. doi:10.3389/fnhum.2014.00327 (PMC4034154)
findings.design: Three human psychoacoustic experiments (music, nature and speech scenes) plus a Kalman-filter computational model.
findings.effect: The abstract reports no effect size. The model scored AUC about 0.71 in the later Huang & Elhilali 2017 benchmark.
findings.rule: What counts is an element's distance from the statistics the bed has set up, not its absolute features. An element whose pitch, level and timbre sit inside the bed's established range is cheap; one outside it on any dimension is costly. No number is supported.
findings.engine: Bed voicing (defines the statistics); element design limits; Sensory Guard
findings.verification_note: I opened PMC4034154 and checked the DOI via Crossref. The abstract says the model 'flags any deviation from background statistics as salient' and 'argues for a potential role of predictive coding', so the authors offer predictive coding as a hypothesis. Correction to design: the paper includes three behavioural experiments, not just a model tested on existing data.

findings.claim: Timbre deviants capture attention in proportion to their size. A distractor that is brighter (higher spectral centroid) or rougher than its neighbours slows the task roughly linearly. The deviation is symmetric (a darker deviant costs as much as a brighter one). Combining brightness and roughness was reported as additive in Exp 5, but the paper's own discussion calls it possibly non-additive.
findings.sources: Bouvier B, Susini P, Marquis-Favre C, Misdariis N (2023). Revealing the stimulus-driven component of attention through modulations of auditory salience by timbre attributes. Sci Rep 13. doi:10.1038/s41598-023-33496-2 (PMC10133446)
findings.design: Lab study, 5 experiments, N=15/20/20/19/19 (93 in total). Sequences of harmonic sounds at 230 ms IOI with a singleton distractor (additional-singleton paradigm).
findings.effect: Exp 1: a singleton with centroid 822 Hz among 512 Hz neighbours added 137 ms of RT (985 to 1121 ms), t(14)=8.33, d=2.1. Errors rose from 16.2% to 24.2% (d=1.0). Brightness slope 14.0 ms per JND (5% centroid step); roughness slope 12.4 ms per JND (10% AM-depth step, 50 Hz AM). Exp 5 combined slope 8.5 ms per JND. The effect was symmetric for brighter and darker deviants (Exp 4). The tested deviations were 1, 2, 5 and 10 JND.
findings.task: Auditory search with a target-duration judgement
findings.rule: Salience cost grows with an element's centroid or roughness distance from its neighbours, in both directions, by roughly 12-14 ms of slowing per JND in this paradigm. Keep new elements' centroid as close to the surrounding material as possible. There is no free zone: the smallest tested deviation (1 JND, about 5%) already falls on the cost slope, so '1 JND is safe' is not supported. Do not use AM-depth roughness to distinguish elements. Whether the two attributes add up is unresolved.
findings.engine: Brightness and spectral targets; element voicing; Sensory Guard
findings.verification_note: I opened PMC10133446. Every number matches. Corrections: (1) the paper contradicts itself on additivity. Exp 5 results say 'additive', but the General Discussion and Conclusion say 'non-additive', so I softened the claim. (2) The rule's 'within about 1 JND is fine' threshold is not in the paper. Costs were linear from 1 JND upward, with no tested safe zone below 1 JND, so I removed it.

findings.claim: A single low harmonic is heard as a separate tone once it is mistuned by about 1-3%. Longer durations make this much easier.
findings.sources: Moore BCJ, Glasberg BR, Peters RW (1986). Thresholds for hearing mistuned partials as separate tones in harmonic complexes. J Acoust Soc Am 80(2):479-483. doi:10.1121/1.394043
findings.design: Lab psychophysics, small N, adaptive threshold. Complexes of 10-12 equal-amplitude components at 60 dB SPL per component; F0 100, 200 or 400 Hz.
findings.effect: At 410 ms, thresholds were about 1-3% of the harmonic frequency, varying by subject; they were higher for the first two harmonics of a 100 Hz F0. Shortening from 1610 ms to 50 ms raised thresholds 3-5 fold.
findings.task: Discriminating a harmonic complex from one with a mistuned partial heard out
findings.rule: For sustained tones, an individual low partial that deviates by about 1% or more from exact harmonic ratios can be heard out as its own tone. Keep synthesized partials of a single voice harmonically locked. This concerns inharmonicity within one voice, not detune or chorus between whole voices, which this study does not address.
findings.engine: How the beds are voiced (partial tuning)
findings.verification_note: I opened the MIT-hosted PDF: 10-12 components, 60 dB/component, 1-3% at 410 ms, and a 3-5x increase from 1610 to 50 ms all match. I could not verify the 'average of about 1.1% for the first four harmonics', so I removed it. I narrowed the rule, because the original extended it to detune or chorus between whole voices, which the paper does not test.

findings.claim: Onset asynchrony separates a component from a sound. A few tens of ms let a harmonic be heard out and removed from vowel quality, but over 100 ms is needed to remove it from the pitch of the whole. Below 1% mistuning suffices to hear it out, about 3% lets it be lateralised separately, and about 8% is needed to substantially cut its contribution to pitch and vowel quality.
findings.sources: Darwin CJ, Hill NI (1993). ASA 125th meeting, Ottawa, abstract 2pMU2, https://auditory.org/asamtgs/asa93ott/2pMU/2pMU2.html. Darwin CJ, Ciocca V (1992). J Acoust Soc Am 91:3381-3390 (not opened). Darwin CJ (1997). Trends Cogn Sci 1(9):327-333 (review).
findings.design: Lab psychophysics, small N (conference abstract plus journal papers)
findings.effect: Hearing out a harmonic: 'a few tens of ms' asynchrony or less than 1% mistuning. Removal from vowel quality: a few tens of ms asynchrony. Removal from pitch: over 100 ms asynchrony, or about 8% mistuning. The 300 ms figure is unverified (Darwin & Ciocca not opened).
findings.rule: A layer meant to merge with the bed should start in close sync with a bed event (well under 'a few tens of ms' off), or fade in with no definable onset. An element that starts on its own, tens of ms off the bed's events, can be heard out as a separate object. The exact '20-30 ms' window is not given by the source.
findings.engine: Element fade-ins (entry timing relative to bed events); bed voicing
findings.verification_note: I opened the Darwin & Hill abstract, and the quotes match: 'a few tens of milliseconds', 'over 100 ms', '<1%', '~3%' and 'around 8%'. I added that a few tens of ms also removes a harmonic from vowel quality. I could not open Darwin & Ciocca 1992 (my search budget ran out), so the 300 ms figure stays unverified. I removed the specific '20-30 ms' window from the rule, since the source says only 'a few tens of ms'.

findings.claim: Temporal coherence binds sounds into one stream. Tones even 15 semitones apart are heard as one stream when synchronous and as two when they alternate, although the neurons stay tonotopically separate.
findings.sources: Elhilali M, Ma L, Micheyl C, Oxenham AJ, Shamma SA (2009). Neuron 61(2):317-329. doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2008.12.005 (PMC2673083). Shamma SA, Elhilali M, Micheyl C (2011). Trends Neurosci 34(3):114-123.
findings.design: Psychophysics (N=9), ferret A1 physiology (122 units in 4 ferrets), computational model, plus a review
findings.effect: Temporal-shift detection thresholds were 2-4 ms when synchronous and 10-20 ms when asynchronous; the paper reports F(1,10)=7.394 with p<0.001, which is internally inconsistent (p is about .02). Model λ2/λ1 was 0.01 (synchronous) vs. 0.93 (alternating).
findings.rule: Elements that share the bed's temporal envelope (same swells, same rhythmic grid, changes at the same moments) tend to fuse into one background even when far apart in frequency. Elements with independent timing segregate. No number is supported beyond synchrony at the ms scale.
findings.engine: Bed voicing (shared modulation across layers); element envelopes locked to the tide or bed
findings.verification_note: I opened PMC2673083. N=9, 122 units, 15 semitones, 2-4 vs. 10-20 ms, and λ ratios of 0.01/0.93 are all present. The paper's own statistics are odd: F(1,10) with N=9, and p<0.001 does not fit F=7.39. That is a reporting issue in the source, not in the finding. The physiology figure values are less clean than the two-tone model values.

findings.claim: Comodulation masking release: noise bands across frequency that share one amplitude modulation group together, and a tone signal not sharing that modulation becomes easier to detect.
findings.sources: Hall JW, Haggard MP, Fernandes MA (1984). Detection in noise by spectro-temporal pattern analysis. J Acoust Soc Am 76(1):50-56. doi:10.1121/1.391005. Review: Verhey JL, Pressnitzer D, Winter IM (2003). Exp Brain Res 153(4):405-417. doi:10.1007/s00221-003-1607-1
findings.design: Lab psychophysics; review
findings.effect: Masking release (threshold improvement) when flanking bands are comodulated. dB magnitude not verified.
findings.rule: Common modulation across bed layers helps them group as one object and can make an unmodulated signal easier to detect. Transfer to musical elements against a slowly swelling bed is an extrapolation. The rule 'every element must follow the swell or sit well below it' is not supported by CMR data, and no dB figure is supported.
findings.engine: Bed voicing (comodulation of layers); element envelopes; tide period
findings.verification_note: I confirmed both citations via Crossref (titles, volumes, pages, DOIs). CMR itself is textbook-level and replicated. I softened the rule: CMR concerns detection thresholds of tones in noise with modulation rates of several Hz and more. A prescription for slow tide-rate swells and elements is an extrapolation.

findings.claim: In multi-source tone scenes, a source disappearing is hard to notice and gets worse as the scene grows. A source appearing is detected near ceiling regardless of scene size, but only when the onset carries a loudness change; when loudness cues were masked, or the change fell in a gap, appearance detection also fell with scene size.
findings.sources: Cervantes Constantino F, Pinggera L, Paranamana S, Kashino M, Chait M (2012). Detection of appearing and disappearing objects in complex acoustic scenes. PLoS ONE 7(9):e46167. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0046167. Sohoglu E, Chait M (2016). eLife 5:e19113.
findings.design: Lab, 7 experiments, N=5-12 each; scenes of 4-14 concurrent tone components
findings.effect: Exp 2: appearance showed no scene-size effect, F(5,30)=2.81, p=.10. Disappearance fell sharply, F(5,30)=31.9, p<.001. Exp 3A (loudness-masked): appearance DID fall with scene size, F(5,45)=17.7, p<.001. Exp 6 (gaps): appearance fell too, F(2,18)=13.3, p<.001.
findings.rule: Entries cost attention far more than exits; weight the change budget toward entries. In beds of about 8 or more components, a removal is hard to detect. Entries are noticed even in dense beds largely through the level step they create. An entry whose loudness change is masked by the bed's own level fluctuation, or that happens across a gap, is less detectable as the bed gets denser.
findings.engine: Change budget weighting (entry vs. exit); element fade-ins vs. fade-outs
findings.verification_note: I opened the PLoS ONE paper. The Exp 2 statistics are confirmed. The finding omitted that the appearance ceiling does not hold in Exp 3A (loudness changes masked) or Exp 6 (gaps), where appearance detection also declined with scene size. That matters for an engine that uses fades and level fluctuation, so I narrowed the claim and rule. Exp 2 had N=7.

findings.claim: Regular (predictable) patterns do not capture attention: regular distractors disrupt less than random ones. But in regular scenes a newly appearing source is detected faster and more accurately.
findings.sources: Southwell R, Baumann A, Gal C, Barascud N, Friston K, Chait M (2017). Is predictability salient? A study of attentional capture by auditory patterns. Phil Trans R Soc B 372:20160105 (PMC5206273). Sohoglu E, Chait M (2016). Detecting and representing predictable structure during auditory scene analysis. eLife 5:e19113.
findings.design: EEG (N=21 of 23) plus behavioural experiments (N=10 and 11); MEG and behaviour in Sohoglu & Chait
findings.effect: Random distractors were more disruptive: RT F=8.06, p=.019; d' F=9.79, p=.012. EEG power was about 30% (27.5-36.7%) higher for regular sequences. Regular sequences gave no hit-rate advantage when monitored (0.65 vs. 0.67). Sohoglu & Chait: appearance was detected more accurately and faster in regular scenes.
findings.task: Change and gap detection with distractors
findings.rule: Regular kick and tick patterns make a cheaper background than random or jittered ones. The price is that a regular bed makes a new entrant easier to notice, so the more regular the bed, the more gradual entries should be. No number is supported.
findings.engine: Kick/tick regularity; element fade-ins; change budget
findings.verification_note: I opened PMC5206273. The N values, F and p values and EEG percentages match, and the abstract states 'regularity does not capture attention'. I confirmed the Sohoglu & Chait 2016 finding via the eLife abstract. Both papers are from the Chait lab, so 'replicated' means converging, not independent, evidence.

findings.claim: Rising intensity can act as a warning cue. Compared with falling intensity, it strengthens orienting and phasic alertness and activates the amygdala. Rising sounds are often judged to change more than equivalent falling sounds, but the bias depends on intensity region: at low intensities, decreases were judged larger than increases.
findings.sources: Neuhoff JG (1998). Perceptual bias for rising tones. Nature 395(6698):123-124. doi:10.1038/25862. Bach DR, Schächinger H, Neuhoff JG, et al. (2008). Rising sound intensity: an intrinsic warning cue activating the amygdala. Cereb Cortex 18(1):145-150. doi:10.1093/cercor/bhm040. Olsen KN, Stevens CJ (2010). Perceptual overestimation of rising intensity: is stimulus continuity necessary? Perception 39(5):695-704. doi:10.1068/p6592
findings.design: Psychophysics; fMRI plus psychophysiology; Olsen & Stevens psychophysics N=30
findings.effect: Rising > falling for orienting, alertness and amygdala BOLD (Bach), with no effect sizes seen. Olsen & Stevens: at high intensities increases were judged larger than decreases; at low intensities with balanced end levels, decreases were judged larger.
findings.task: Passive listening, loudness-change judgement, target detection
findings.rule: Treat every fade-in as a potential warning event and keep its absolute level rise small relative to the bed, spread over time. At the low levels a focus engine uses, the perceptual overestimation of rises may not hold (it reversed in one study), so the main risk is the orienting response, not perceived magnitude. No rate or range number is supported.
findings.engine: Element fade-ins (rise range and rate); Sensory Guard
findings.verification_note: I confirmed the citations via Crossref and Europe PMC. Bach et al. is print 2008, Cereb Cortex 18(1):145-150; the finding had no volume or pages. I located the 'challenge' paper: Olsen & Stevens 2010, Perception 39(5):695-704. Its abstract says the rising-intensity bias appeared at high intensities but reversed at low intensities, which is directly relevant to a low-level engine. I added this and adjusted the rule.

findings.claim: Longer onset rise times reduce reflexive startle. In humans, startle blink magnitude falls as rise time increases, for loud stimuli. In odontocetes, modelled startle disappears at rise times of about 140 ms in one animal and over 220 ms in another.
findings.sources: Blumenthal TD (1988). The startle response to acoustic stimuli near startle threshold: effects of stimulus rise and fall time, duration, and intensity. Psychophysiology 25(5):607-611. doi:10.1111/j.1469-8986.1988.tb01897.x. Ramírez I, Sánchez MB, Fernández MC, Lipp OV, Vila J (2005). Psychophysiology 42(6):732-739. doi:10.1111/j.1469-8986.2005.00362.x. Götz T, Pacini AF, Nachtigall PE, Janik VM (2020). J Exp Biol 223:jeb208470 (PMC7075047).
findings.design: Human lab startle (Ramírez: two studies of N=100 each, 105 dB white noise); Götz: 3 animals (2 bottlenose dolphins, 1 false killer whale)
findings.effect: Ramírez: rise time altered blink startle (per Götz, magnitude 'decreased linearly with increasing stimulus rise time'), and weak responses can persist at 100 ms rise for loud broadband stimuli. Götz: about 1.1% less startle per ms in one dolphin; a linear decrease in a second; non-significant in the false killer whale. Modelled abolition was a mean 141 ms (94-189 ms across sessions) in one animal and over 220 ms in another. Blumenthal 1988: abstract not seen; numbers not confirmed.
findings.population: Adults (human, loud stimuli); 2 dolphins and 1 false killer whale
findings.rule: Direction is clear: slower attacks mean less reflexive response. These data come from 105 dB stimuli and animals, far above an engine's levels, so they give only a direction. For low-level orienting no rise-time number is supported; 'a few hundred ms' for non-percussive entries is a heuristic.
findings.engine: Element fade-ins (attack time); kick/tick envelope design
findings.verification_note: I confirmed Blumenthal 1988 exists (Europe PMC: Psychophysiology 25(5):607-611), but I could not read its abstract. Götz cites Blumenthal & Berg 1986 for the classic 'onset under 15-25 ms' startle criterion. The finding's 'N=60 at 80-85 dBA' and 'rise times 0-240 ms' are unverified, so I removed them. I confirmed Ramírez via Crossref (two studies of N=100, 105 dB). I opened Götz: the abolition values are per animal, the 1.1%/ms is for one animal only, and the false killer whale result was not significant.

findings.claim: At equal energy, 'ramped' sounds (slow rise, fast decay) are judged louder than 'damped' sounds (fast attack, slow decay); they are also heard as longer.
findings.sources: Stecker GC, Hafter ER (2000). An effect of temporal asymmetry on loudness. J Acoust Soc Am 107(6):3358-3368. doi:10.1121/1.429407. Grassi M, Darwin CJ (2006). The subjective duration of ramped and damped sounds. Percept Psychophys 68(8):1382-1392. doi:10.3758/BF03193737
findings.design: Lab psychophysics
findings.effect: Slow-onset/fast-decay sounds were judged louder than their time-reversed equivalents, for sinusoidal and noise carriers. The effect depended on stimulus order and was largest after a damped sound. dB magnitude not verified.
findings.rule: Damped envelopes (pluck- or bell-like decay) sound quieter and shorter than reversed, swelled envelopes of the same energy. A swell that cuts off at its peak is the conspicuous shape. Let element envelopes decay gradually. No dB number is supported.
findings.engine: Element envelope shape (fade-out tails); kick/tick envelopes
findings.verification_note: I confirmed Stecker & Hafter 2000 via the Crossref abstract (volume 107(6), pages 3358-3368, added) and Grassi & Darwin 2006 via Crossref metadata (68(8):1382-1392). I did not open the hal-01106575 follow-up, so its 'slight / reverses at high intensity' description is unverified and I dropped it from the sources.

findings.claim: Amplitude modulation at about 30-150 Hz (roughness) is the acoustic signature of screams and alarms. It increases perceived fear, speeds responses and engages the amygdala.
findings.sources: Arnal LH, Flinker A, Kleinschmidt A, Giraud AL, Poeppel D (2015). Human screams occupy a privileged niche in the communication soundscape. Curr Biol 25(15):2051-2056. doi:10.1016/j.cub.2015.06.043 (PMC4562283). Extension: Arnal LH, Kleinschmidt A, Spinelli L, Giraud AL, Mégevand P (2019). The rough sound of salience enhances aversion through neural synchronisation. Nat Commun (PMC6694125).
findings.design: Acoustic analysis of vocalisations from 19 speakers, behavioural ratings and localisation, fMRI (N=16)
findings.effect: Roughness correlated with fear ratings r=0.65 (p=1e-8) and with faster responses r=-0.35 (p=.005). Adding roughness to neutral voices raised fear (p=.045). Alarms were rougher than instruments (p=9e-10).
findings.rule: No bed or element should carry amplitude modulation or beating in the 30-150 Hz range. Two voices within one critical band whose frequencies differ by 30-150 Hz beat in that range, so avoid such pairings in the low and mid register. Slow detune (a few Hz or less) falls outside this range.
findings.engine: Bed voicing (detune and interval spacing); Sensory Guard (roughness check)
findings.verification_note: I opened PMC4562283. 19 speakers, fMRI N=16, r=0.65, r=-0.35, p=.045 and p=9e-10 all match. The 2019 Nat Commun follow-up from the same group (seen as a search hit) extends the aversion finding, so I changed replication to 'replicated' (same lab). The detune-to-beating step in the rule is a psychoacoustic inference, not tested in the paper.

findings.claim: Modulation is heard as fluctuation, peaking at about 4 Hz, and turns into roughness from about 15-20 Hz, peaking at about 70 Hz for a 1 kHz carrier. Two pure tones are most dissonant at a separation of about a quarter of a critical bandwidth.
findings.sources: Fastl H, Zwicker E. Psychoacoustics: Facts and Models (Springer). Plomp R, Levelt WJM (1965). Tonal consonance and critical bandwidth. J Acoust Soc Am 38:548-560. doi:10.1121/1.1909741
findings.design: Psychoacoustic textbook synthesis; lab rating study (Plomp & Levelt)
findings.effect: Fluctuation strength peaks at about 4 Hz and roughness at about 70 Hz. Maximum dissonance is at about 25% of critical bandwidth. The 'Greenwood: about 40%' revision is unverified.
findings.rule: Keep slow bed motion well below the 2-8 Hz band where fluctuation is most prominent. Avoid AM in the roughness range (about 15-300 Hz). In the bass, critical bands are wide relative to note spacing, so seconds and thirds become rough; voice the low register in open intervals (fifths, octaves). The '<1 Hz' figure for tide motion is a design choice, not a measured threshold.
findings.engine: How the beds are voiced (register spacing); tide period / LFO rates; Sensory Guard
findings.verification_note: My search budget ran out before I could open these sources. The fluctuation (4 Hz) and roughness (70 Hz) peaks and Plomp-Levelt's quarter-critical-band maximum are textbook values I am confident of, and the Plomp & Levelt DOI is standard. I removed the 'Greenwood ~40%' figure because I could not verify it, and flagged the '<1 Hz' tide figure as a design choice.

findings.claim: For everyday sounds, a small set of psychoacoustic metrics (sharpness and roughness, with loudness in one report) explains about 94-98% of perceived unpleasantness, while A-weighted level does not predict it.
findings.sources: Ellermeier W, Mader M, Daniel P (1997). Perceived unpleasantness of natural sounds: ratio-scale measurement and psychoacoustic analysis. J Acoust Soc Am 102(5 Suppl):3191. doi:10.1121/1.420881 (abstract). Journal version: Ellermeier, Mader & Daniel (2004), Acta Acustica united with Acustica (not located). Zimmer K, Ellermeier W, Schmid C (2004). Revealing criteria which underlie judgments of auditory unpleasantness. J Acoust Soc Am 115(5 Suppl):2604. doi:10.1121/1.4784647
findings.design: Lab paired comparisons, N=60 (10 natural sounds); companion N=74 (12 sounds)
findings.effect: 1997 abstract: scale values spanned a factor of 100, dBA did not predict them, and a linear combination of LOUDNESS, roughness and sharpness explained 98% of the variance. Zimmer 2004: within sound subgroups, sharpness and roughness explained unpleasantness (r² corrected = 0.96). R² > 0.94 for roughness plus sharpness alone is unverified.
findings.rule: Comfort metrics for a Sensory Guard should include sharpness and roughness alongside psychoacoustic loudness, not just dBA. A-weighted level is a poor proxy, but loudness (sone) still contributes. Evidence is from short environmental clips, from one lab.
findings.engine: Sensory Guard (metrics: sharpness, roughness, loudness); brightness and spectral targets
findings.verification_note: I could not reach the Regensburg record (connection refused) and could not find the 2004 Acta Acustica paper via Crossref. I found the 1997 JASA abstract by the same authors, with the same design (60 listeners, 10 sounds): it says loudness, roughness AND sharpness explained 98%. That contradicts the finding's 'level matters less / sharpness+roughness alone'. I found the companion as a JASA abstract (r²corr=0.96 within subgroups). Both reports are from the Ellermeier lab.

findings.claim: Sound unpleasantness maps onto energy at 2500-5500 Hz combined with temporal modulation at 1-16 Hz.
findings.sources: Kumar S, Forster HM, Bailey P, Griffiths TD (2008). Mapping unpleasantness of sounds to their auditory representation. J Acoust Soc Am 124(6):3810-3817. doi:10.1121/1.3006380 (PMID 19206807)
findings.design: Lab ratings of many sounds, including grating sounds; a PLS model on an auditory-model representation, validated on new sounds
findings.effect: Unpleasantness 'existence region' at 2500-5500 Hz and 1-16 Hz modulation. The abstract gives no N or effect size.
findings.rule: Keep the 2.5-5.5 kHz region low in level and free of 1-16 Hz modulation (no fluttery shimmer, tremolo or strong tick trains there). Moving tick or hat energy out of that band is an extrapolation from short, highly unpleasant clips.
findings.engine: Brightness and spectral targets (2.5-5.5 kHz ceiling); kick/tick timbre; Sensory Guard
findings.verification_note: I confirmed the abstract via Europe PMC: the citation, the 2500-5500 Hz and 1-16 Hz ranges, and the absence of an N are all correct. The stimuli were dominated by aversive sounds such as scraping, so transfer to quiet music is uncertain.

findings.claim: The Zwicker/Fastl psychoacoustic annoyance index scales loudness (N5) by a combination of sharpness, fluctuation strength and roughness. Its sharpness term applies only above 1.75 acum.
findings.sources: Fastl H, Zwicker E, Psychoacoustics: Facts and Models (Springer). Formula: https://metricgate.com/docs/psychoacoustic-annoyance/ (practitioner).
findings.design: Model and standard (practitioner use)
findings.effect: PA = N5(1 + sqrt(wS² + wFR²)), with wS = (S - 1.75)·0.25·log10(N5 + 10) when S > 1.75 acum, and wFR = 2.18/N5^0.4 · (0.4F + 0.6R). No validation effect sizes were found.
findings.rule: A sharpness ceiling of about 1.75 acum is a defensible Sensory Guard default only as a model convention, not as an empirical comfort threshold. Lower is safer.
findings.engine: Sensory Guard (sharpness ceiling); brightness targets
findings.verification_note: I opened the metricgate page and confirmed the formula and the 1.75 acum switch-on. I removed the parenthetical '(roughly the sharpness of broadband noise)', which is unverified. I did not open the aircraft-noise validation reports.

findings.claim: At the same A-weighted level (40 dBA), low-frequency-dominated ventilation noise was rated more annoying and more work-disruptive than a flat spectrum, and in high-noise-sensitive people it attenuated the normal daily decline of cortisol. A-weighting underestimates low-frequency effects.
findings.sources: Persson Waye K, Bengtsson J, Rylander R, Hucklebridge F, Evans P, Clow A (2002). Low frequency noise enhances cortisol among noise sensitive subjects during work performance. Life Sci 70(7):745-758. doi:10.1016/S0024-3205(01)01450-3. Leventhall HG (2004). Low frequency noise and annoyance. Noise Health 6(23):59-72 (review).
findings.design: Lab study, N=32, 2 h of performance tasks at 40 dBA (LF-dominant vs. flat ventilation noise); narrative review
findings.effect: LF noise was rated more annoying and more work-disruptive. The cortisol decline was attenuated only in the high-noise-sensitive subgroup. No standardised effect sizes in the abstract.
findings.rule: Do not let bass energy (about 20-200 Hz) dominate the bed. The Sensory Guard should measure low-frequency energy directly (unweighted or C-weighted), not only via dBA. No dB cap is supported for headphone music beds.
findings.engine: Brightness and spectral targets (low-frequency share); kick level/tuning; Sensory Guard
findings.verification_note: I confirmed the Persson Waye abstract via Europe PMC: N=32, 2 h, 40 dBA, the annoyance and work-disruption results, and the cortisol effect in high-sensitive subjects only. I did not reopen the Leventhall review; the citation is standard.

findings.claim: Audible low-frequency tonal components added to broadband noise increase annoyance by the equivalent of 0-7 dB. The penalty rises with tonal audibility up to about 6 dB, then flattens or drops, and it is LARGER for higher tone frequencies (100-400 Hz) than for 40-50 Hz tones.
findings.sources: Yonemura M, Lee H, Sakamoto S (2021). Subjective evaluation on the annoyance of environmental noise containing low-frequency tonal components. Int J Environ Res Public Health 18(13):7127. doi:10.3390/ijerph18137127 (PMC8297235). ISO 1996-2 tone adjustment (not opened).
findings.design: Lab study, 60 recruited and 51 analysed. Tones at 40, 50, 100, 200 and 400 Hz in broadband noise at 25/30/35 dBA; tonal audibility 0-12 dB.
findings.effect: Tonal adjustment of 0-7 dB at 25-30 dBA and 0-5 dB at 35 dBA. It rose with tonal audibility up to about 6 dB, then flattened or fell, most clearly at 40-50 Hz. 'The higher the tonal frequency, the larger the value'. Above 100 Hz, the adjustment was 2-4 dB above the ISO 1996-2 value.
findings.rule: Evidence is from environmental noise in quiet rooms, not musical drones. A sustained pure tone standing about 6 dB or more above its surrounding floor can carry several dB of extra annoyance, more so for tones at 100-400 Hz than at 40-50 Hz. For long drones prefer complex, slightly broadened tones over a single prominent pure tone.
findings.engine: How the beds are voiced (drone purity); Sensory Guard (tonal prominence)
findings.verification_note: I opened PMC8297235. N=51 analysed of 60, the levels, the 0-7 and 0-5 dB ranges and the plateau near 6 dB are confirmed. The finding missed the main frequency result: the penalty grows with tone frequency, and 40-50 Hz tones (near threshold) got the smallest penalty. I added this. I changed replication to 'single study', since nothing else in the finding shows the Yonemura result was reproduced.

findings.claim: The popular claim is that nature sounds such as water and birds make better work backgrounds than engineered noise. A 15-week open-plan field study found no water-based masking sound better than pseudo-random noise. Babbling water and water with bird calls were rated worst, and the spectrally closest water sound (waterfall) did not differ from the noise.
findings.sources: Hongisto V, Varjo J, Oliva D, Haapakangas A, Benway E (2017). Perception of water-based masking sounds: long-term experiment in an open-plan office. Front Psychol 8:1177. doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2017.01177
findings.design: Field study, within-subjects, fixed order, 3-week conditions (18 weeks including the repeated reference). 77 invited, core N=18, 28-47 respondents per condition, about 43-44.6 dB LAeq.
findings.effect: Noise disturbance η²=0.29; pseudo-random noise vs. babbling river d=1.50, vs. river with birds d=1.34. Disturbance by the masking sound itself η²=0.46; acoustic satisfaction η²=0.43. Reference noise slope -5 dB per octave over 125-8000 Hz.
findings.rule: An ambient 'world' layer helps only if it is spectrally steady and close to a gently sloping spectrum (about -5 dB per octave). Babbling or bright water and intermittent identifiable events such as birds raise disturbance. Comfort tracks spectral steadiness, not naturalness. Small core sample and fixed order, so treat this as a caution.
findings.engine: Ambient world layer selection; brightness and spectral targets (slope); change budget for identifiable events
findings.verification_note: I opened the Frontiers paper, and the numbers match. Correction: η²=0.46 is work disturbance caused by the masking sound itself, not general work disturbance. Replication was labelled 'contested' with no contrary study cited, so I changed it to 'single study'. I graded it weak, given core N=18 and a fixed condition order.

findings.claim: Disruption of serial recall by irrelevant speech or music was the same at 60 and 75 dBA. Adding pink noise reduced disruption linearly as the speech-to-noise ratio fell. Binaural unmasking contributed negligibly.
findings.sources: Ellermeier W, Hellbrück J (1998). Is level irrelevant in 'irrelevant speech'? Effects of loudness, signal-to-noise ratio, and binaural unmasking. J Exp Psychol Hum Percept Perform 24(5):1406-1414. doi:10.1037/0096-1523.24.5.1406
findings.design: Lab, 3 experiments, serial recall
