findings.effect: No level effect between 60 and 75 dBA for speech or music. Linear improvement as SNR to the pink-noise floor fell. Binaural unmasking negligible. Exact effect sizes not seen.
findings.task: Visual serial recall with irrelevant sound
findings.rule: The disruption from a changing element is set by its prominence over a steady floor (element-to-bed ratio), not by playback volume. Keep changing or segmented elements low relative to a continuous bed; the bed acts as the protective masker. No SNR target is supported.
findings.engine: Element-to-bed level ratio (fade-in targets); bed continuity; Sensory Guard
findings.verification_note: I confirmed the abstract via Europe PMC: 60 vs. 75 dB(A), the linear SNR improvement with pink noise and negligible binaural unmasking all match. The authors conclude that the 'segmented, changing nature' is crucial, and that uniform masking noise may reduce the effect.

findings.claim: Presenting irrelevant speech items at different stereo locations significantly reduces their disruption (the changing-state effect), but not to the level of a monophonic steady-state stream; location change may itself add some interference.
findings.sources: Kattner F, Hassanzadeh M, Ellermeier W (2024). The role of spatial location in irrelevant speech revisited: a preregistered replication study. J Exp Psychol Learn Mem Cogn 50(12):1892-1900. doi:10.1037/xlm0001424. Original: Jones DM, Macken WJ (1995).
findings.design: Preregistered replication, lab serial recall, N=60
findings.effect: Stereophonic presentation significantly reduced the changing-state effect. Stereophonic sequences remained slightly more disruptive than monophonic steady-state sequences, which the authors attribute to location change. Both were worse than silence. No numerical effect sizes in the abstract.
findings.rule: Giving recurring elements their own fixed pan positions may help them settle into separate steady streams and somewhat reduce disruption. It is a partial measure, not a substitute for a low change rate, and moving between positions carries its own cost. No pan angle is supported.
findings.engine: Panning (fixed per-element positions)
findings.verification_note: I confirmed the citation via Crossref (adding the second author's first initial) and the abstract via Europe PMC: N=60, a significant reduction, still above monophonic steady-state. I added the authors' explanation that location change itself interferes. The preprint and journal wording differ slightly.

findings.claim: Rare, task-irrelevant changes in a sound's spatial location are involuntary distractors: they slow responses and produce MMN, P3a and RON. Location deviants produced more behavioural distraction than duration deviants.
findings.sources: Roeber U, Widmann A, Schröger E (2003). Auditory distraction by duration and location deviants: a behavioral and event-related potential study. Cogn Brain Res 17(2):347-357. doi:10.1016/S0926-6410(03)00136-8
findings.design: Lab ERP study (oddball distraction)
findings.effect: Responses to deviants were slower than to standards in both conditions. Behavioural distraction was 'markedly smaller with duration Deviants'. Distraction also carried over to the next standard. Exact ms not seen.
findings.task: Duration or location discrimination with irrelevant deviants
findings.rule: Do not move an element's pan position while it plays (no auto-pan, no position jumps). Unexpected location changes are strong involuntary distractors. Any spatial change should be extremely slow or happen only while the element is silent.
findings.engine: Panning (static positions; no auto-pan)
findings.verification_note: I confirmed the abstract via Europe PMC: the citation, both deviant types slowing responses, and smaller distraction for duration deviants. Caveat: the authors attribute the asymmetry to processing timing (task × deviant confound), not to location being intrinsically more distracting. That an unpredictable location change distracts is well supported.

findings.claim: Over headphones, sounds are heard inside the head when cues are unnatural. Externalisation improves with binaural (interaurally different) reverberant tails up to about 80 ms, with no gain beyond that. Diotic reverb has little effect. Fast-acting compression that reduces ILDs, and head-fixed sources, reduce externalisation.
findings.sources: Best V, Baumgartner R, Lavandier M, Majdak P, Kopčo N (2020). Sound externalization: a review of recent research. Trends Hear 24:2331216520948390. doi:10.1177/2331216520948390 (PMC7488874)
findings.design: Narrative review of psychoacoustic studies
findings.effect: Externalisation benefit saturates with reverberant tails of about 80 ms (Begault 2001; Catic 2015). Diotic reverb had little effect (Leclère 2019). Fast-acting hearing-aid compression (reduced ILDs) lowered externalisation (Wiggins & Seeber 2012). Head-fixed sources tend to be internalised (Brimijoin 2013). Individual vs. generic HRTFs gave mixed results. Crossfeed is not covered.
findings.rule: To place the mix outside the head on headphones, give elements a short decorrelated (interaurally different) reverb of about 80 ms early tail. Mono or identical-channel reverb will not do it. That hard-panned dry or one-ear elements push sound inside the head is a reasonable inference, not a tested claim in the review.
findings.engine: Panning/stereo width; reverb or space per element; mix as one place
findings.verification_note: I opened PMC7488874, and the reverb, diotic reverb, head-fixed and HRTF statements match. Correction: the 'ILD compression' evidence is fast-acting hearing-aid dynamic-range compression, not compression of natural ILDs in general. The review does not test hard-panning, so I marked that part of the rule as inference.

findings.claim: The popular practitioner claim is that crossfeed reduces fatigue in long headphone sessions and fixes unnatural 'superstereo'. bs2b defaults to 700 Hz cutoff at 4.5 dB feed, described as closest to virtual speakers at 30° and about 3 m. No controlled fatigue study was found.
findings.sources: bs2b project, https://bs2b.sourceforge.net/ (practitioner). Presets: 700 Hz/4.5 dB (default), 700 Hz/6 dB (Chu Moy-like), 650 Hz/9.5 dB (Jan Meier-like).
findings.design: Practitioner design rationale; no controlled listening-fatigue trials found
findings.effect: None reported. The site asserts that superstereo causes fatigue and that crossfeed is 'helpful for prolonged headphone listening', with no data.
findings.rule: If the mix has wide or hard-panned content, a mild crossfeed (about 700 Hz, 4.5-6 dB) is a low-risk default, but its fatigue benefit is unproven. A simpler route is to avoid hard pans.
findings.engine: Panning/stereo width; headphone output stage (crossfeed toggle)
findings.verification_note: I opened bs2b.sourceforge.net. The defaults, presets, the 30°/3 m description and the unsupported fatigue claim all match.

findings.claim: The WHO-ITU safe listening standard sets a weekly sound allowance of 80 dB(A) for 40 hours for adults (Mode 1) and 75 dB(A) for 40 hours for children / sensitive users (Mode 2), based on equal energy.
findings.sources: WHO & ITU (2019). Safe listening devices and systems: a WHO-ITU standard. https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241515276 (corresponds to ITU-T H.870).
findings.design: Consensus standard
findings.effect: n/a (exposure limit). Equal-energy rule: each +3 dB halves the allowed time.
findings.population: Adults and children using personal audio
findings.rule: A user listening 40 h a week must average no more than 80 dB(A) at the ear (75 for Mode 2). Every +3 dB halves the time. An all-day focus engine should default well below this, since the weekly budget is shared with all other listening.
findings.engine: Sensory Guard (output level ceiling and exposure tracking)
findings.verification_note: I opened the WHO page: 'Mode 1 for adults: 80 dB for 40 hours per week; Mode 2 for children: 75 dB'. The page labels Mode 2 as for children; the H.870 standard text also uses 'sensitive users'. The page itself does not mention H.870. As a standard, its grade reflects authority, not experimental evidence.

findings.claim: Background music has no net effect on adult performance overall because specific effects cancel. It disturbs reading, has small detrimental effects on memory, has a positive effect on emotional reactions and sport, and its tempo sets the tempo of the concurrent activity.
findings.sources: Kämpfe, Sedlmeier & Renkewitz (2011; online Nov 2010). The impact of background music on adult listeners: a meta-analysis. Psychology of Music 39(4):424-448. doi:10.1177/0305735610376261
findings.design: Meta-analysis (number of studies not verified; abstract only)
findings.effect: Global effect about null; specific effects average out. Reading disturbed; small detrimental memory effect; positive for emotion and sport; tempo of music shifts tempo of activity. No sizes verified. Authors say power was low because few studies allowed effect sizes.
findings.rule: Do not assume sound improves cognition by default. For reading or memory jobs, expect a small cost from music. Tempo pulls action pace with it. No number supported.
findings.engine: Tempo per job; Character dial (default low for Read)
findings.verification_note: Abstract confirmed via search (sagepub record and gwern PDF listing). All directional claims match the abstract. Downgraded strong to moderate: the authors themselves say few studies allowed effect sizes, so the chance of detecting specific effects was low. Note that Thompson et al. 2012 (C3-07) found slow or soft music did not disrupt reading, which qualifies 'disturbs reading'.

findings.claim: A systematic review of 95 articles (154 experiments) found background music mostly has no effect. Where there is an effect, it is detrimental for memory and language tasks (lyrics worse), appears with difficult but not easy tasks, and with introverts but not extraverts. Only one positive effect was found.
findings.sources: Cheah, Wong, Spitzer & Coutinho (2022). Background Music and Cognitive Task Performance: A Systematic Review of Task, Music, and Population Impact. Music & Science 5. doi:10.1177/20592043221134392. PROSPERO CRD42020207193
findings.design: Systematic review (PRISMA/SWiM), 95 articles, 154 experiments, six domains; vote-count synthesis, no pooled ES
findings.effect: Most comparisons null; detrimental for memory and language, lyrics worse; one positive effect; harm with difficult tasks and introverts
findings.rule: Scale stimulation down as task difficulty and verbal load rise: Read/Write get the lowest event density. No number supported.
findings.engine: Character dial; kick and tick density per job (Read, Write vs Hours, Hold)
findings.verification_note: Citation, DOI and abstract content confirmed (Liverpool repository and search abstract). Grade lowered from strong to moderate: the synthesis is a vote count without pooled effect sizes, and the introvert moderator rests on the contested personality literature (see C3-25).

findings.claim: Tempo raises self-reported arousal; mode changes mood, not arousal. Better spatial scores after fast/major Mozart are explained by arousal and mood (arousal-mood hypothesis).
findings.sources: Husain, Thompson & Schellenberg (2002). Effects of musical tempo and mode on arousal, mood, and spatial abilities. Music Perception 20(2):151-171. Thompson, Schellenberg & Husain (2001). Arousal, mood, and the Mozart effect. Psychological Science 12(3):248-251
findings.design: Lab between-subjects, N=36 (8-9 per cell); Mozart K.448 at 165 vs 60 bpm, major vs minor; 10 min of listening BEFORE the task (not background); POMS factor scores
findings.effect: Tempo on arousal change F(1,32)=91.82, p<.001 (ηp² about 0.74 computed). Tempo on spatial score F(1,32)=44.81; mode F(1,32)=8.45. Mode on mood F(1,32)=17.16; mode on arousal n.s.
findings.task: Paper folding and cutting after listening
findings.rule: Tempo is the main arousal lever; mode/harmony is the mood lever. 60 vs 165 bpm were extremes chosen as the slowest and fastest that 'still sounded natural', not optimal values.
findings.engine: Tempo per job; state changes Settle -> Deep -> Energise
findings.verification_note: Read the Husain PDF (UTM site): N=36, 165/60 bpm, F(1,32)=91.82 for tempo on arousal, F=44.81 for tempo on PF&C, mode affected mood not arousal, all confirmed. Caveat added: music preceded the task (not concurrent), and cells were tiny (8-9).

findings.claim: Tempo, accentuation and rhythmic articulation best discriminate high from low arousal and correlate most with physiology. Music that raised breathing rate, ventilation, skin conductance and heart rate was fast, accentuated and staccato.
findings.sources: Gomez & Danuser (2007). Relationships between musical structure and psychophysiological measures of emotion. Emotion 7(2):377-387. doi:10.1037/1528-3542.7.2.377
findings.design: Lab, 16 excerpts x 11 structural features; respiration, SCL, HR; correlational (N not verified)
findings.effect: Tempo, accentuation and rhythmic articulation were the strongest correlates of arousal ratings and physiology (no single ES verified)
findings.rule: Accent strength and articulation (sharp, staccato transients) are arousal cues alongside tempo; softer, legato hits read lower. The study is correlational over 16 excerpts where features covary, so it does not show these act independently of BPM. No number supported.
findings.engine: Kick and tick density and accent/attack; Character dial
findings.verification_note: Abstract confirmed. Removed 'independently of BPM' from the rule: 16 natural excerpts with covarying features cannot separate accent from tempo.

findings.claim: Music induces arousal mainly through tempo (faster tempo raises ventilation, BP, HR), not through style or preference. A randomly inserted 2-min pause (silence) reduced HR, BP and minute ventilation even below baseline. No autonomic habituation was seen.
findings.sources: Bernardi, Porta & Sleight (2006). Cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, and respiratory changes induced by different types of music in musicians and non-musicians: the importance of silence. Heart 92(4):445-452. doi:10.1136/hrt.2005.064600 (PMC1860846)
findings.design: Lab, 12 musicians + 12 controls; 6 styles; random 2-min silent pause
findings.effect: Arousal 'predominantly related to the tempo'; 'all variables were related to the tempo but not to music preference'. Pause reduced HR, BP and minute ventilation below baseline. No habituation except cerebral blood flow.
findings.rule: A silent gap after rhythmic music is a strong short-term de-arousal event. Whether a drop-out of only the beat (bed continues) does the same is untested; treat it as a hypothesis for Settle.
findings.engine: State changes (Settle); fades; kick and tick drop-outs
findings.verification_note: PMC abstract and discussion quoted. The pause was full silence, not 'the bed alone', so the rule's '2 min of bed alone' overreaches. 'Simpler rhythm' is not in the abstract (from editorial commentary). Replication changed to single study since I found no independent replication.

findings.claim: No studies show heart rate entraining to musical beats. Exciting music raises HR and respiratory rate relative to tranquilising music; effects on the heart are small and studies inhomogeneous.
findings.sources: Koelsch & Jäncke (2015). Music and the heart. European Heart Journal 36(44):3043-3048. doi:10.1093/eurheartj/ehv430
findings.design: Narrative review
findings.effect: No evidence of HR entrainment to beat; exciting > tranquilising music for HR and RR; effects small and inhomogeneous
findings.rule: Do not set BPM to match or pull resting heart rate. Treat tempo as a general arousal cue only.
findings.engine: Tempo per job
findings.verification_note: Confirmed via RERO repository record and abstract quotes. Page range is 3043-3048 (finding said 3049); minor.

findings.claim: Background music that is both fast and loud disrupts reading comprehension below silence; slow/soft, slow/loud and fast/soft do not.
findings.sources: Thompson, Schellenberg & Letnic (2012). Fast and loud background music disrupts reading comprehension. Psychology of Music 40(6):700-708
findings.design: Lab within-subjects, N=25 + separate silent baseline n=16; 110 vs 150 bpm x 60 vs 72.4 dB (at headphones); Mozart K.448
findings.effect: Tempo x intensity F(1,23)=8.14, p<.01. Fast/loud M=1.95 vs baseline 2.77 (t(39)=2.37, p<.05). Fast/soft 2.96, slow/soft 2.38, slow/loud 2.43 (n.s. vs baseline).
findings.rule: For Read, do not combine high tempo with high level. In a 9-person pilot, a 110-to-150 bpm change was judged equivalent to a 60-to-72.4 dB change, so loudness and tempo trade off, but that equivalence is rough.
findings.engine: Tempo per job (Read); Character dial; Sensory Guard
findings.verification_note: Read the PDF text: all statistics confirmed. Correction: the 12.4 dB = 40 bpm equivalence came from a pilot of N=9 rating 5-s excerpts, so it should not be treated as a precise exchange rate. The baseline was a between-subjects comparison with n=16.

findings.claim: Slow-tempo music (66 bpm) gave slower processing speed and worse scores than no music on three speeded tasks; fast tempo (138 bpm) did not differ from silence. Arousal did not mediate. Exception: slow tempo gave higher accuracy on the linguistic task.
findings.sources: Lin, Kuo & Mai (2023). Slower tempo makes worse performance? The effect of musical tempo on cognitive processing speed. Frontiers in Psychology 14:998460. doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2023.998460
findings.design: Lab between-subjects, N=51 (slow 18, fast 20, silence 13); Mozart K.448 Andante time-stretched
findings.effect: η² 0.30-0.58 (reported as η², not ηp²) for RT and score. Arousal indirect effect -0.093, 95% CI [-0.561, 0.339]. Letter matching accuracy: slow 93.4% vs silence 87.1%, fast 89.9%. Text and tables report some differing F values.
findings.task: Choice RT, visual search, letter matching
findings.rule: Very slow tempo may slow speeded work, possibly as a speed-accuracy shift (more accurate on the verbal task). Fast tempo added nothing over silence. Small groups; provisional.
findings.engine: Tempo per job; state changes (Settle vs Energise)
findings.verification_note: PMC full text checked. Added the linguistic accuracy exception (slow tempo more accurate), which the finding omitted; the authors suggest slow music may help accuracy on complex tasks. Effect sizes are η². Noted internal F inconsistencies.

findings.claim: Self-chosen background music on a low-demand vigilance task increased task-focus and decreased mind-wandering without reducing RT; a follow-up showed music raised pupil-indexed arousal and arousal mediated the attentional-state effect.
findings.sources: Kiss & Linnell (2021). The effect of preferred background music on task-focus in sustained attention. Psychological Research 85(6):2313-2325. doi:10.1007/s00426-020-01400-6. Kiss, Szikora & Linnell (2024). Music in the eye of the beholder... Psychological Research 88(5):1616-1628. doi:10.1007/s00426-024-01963-8
findings.design: Lab within-subjects, N=40 and N=39, PVT with thought probes; 2024 adds pupillometry
findings.effect: Music increased task-focus, decreased mind-wandering, no RT or RT-variability benefit; music increased arousal; arousal mediated the effect. Specific statistics (F=4.71, ηp²=.11, b=.554, indirect .024) not verified (paywalled).
findings.population: Students who habitually work to music, using their own music
findings.rule: For long, low-demand jobs, self-chosen stimulation can raise arousal and task-focus but did not improve speed. Neither study manipulated time-on-task, so it does not show that adding stimulation late in a session counters decline.
findings.engine: Character dial; Hours/Hold jobs
findings.verification_note: Both abstracts confirmed (Europe PMC, Crossref). The 'replication' is same-lab conceptual. Numeric stats could not be checked. Removed the tide/late-session extrapolation; the studies tested music vs silence, not stimulation over time. Note that the music was participant-selected, which a generative engine cannot reproduce.

findings.claim: The 'Yerkes-Dodson law' was a 1908 result about stimulus strength and habit formation for tasks of varying discrimination difficulty. Later authors recast it as arousal, anxiety, stress or motivation versus performance, often misattributing this to Yerkes and Dodson.
findings.sources: Teigen (1994). Yerkes-Dodson: A law for all seasons. Theory & Psychology 4(4):525-547. doi:10.1177/0959354394044004
findings.design: Historical and conceptual review
findings.effect: No effect size; documents conceptual drift and vagueness of the constructs
findings.rule: Do not hard-code a single universal arousal optimum. Any inverted U must be set per task and per listener, and calibrated by the listener. No number supported.
findings.engine: Character dial (user-calibrated); state changes
findings.verification_note: Abstract retrieved via Crossref and matches the drift claim. 'Unitary arousal theory is weak' is not in the abstract; it is the researcher's gloss, so I dropped it from the claim.

findings.claim: Most music-preference studies fit a (segmented) inverted U over collative variables such as complexity and familiarity: 50 of 57 studies (87.7%) were compatible.
findings.sources: Chmiel & Schubert (2017). Back to the inverted-U for music preference: a review of the literature. Psychology of Music 45(6):886-909
findings.design: Literature review, vote count of 57 studies
findings.effect: 50 compatible (87.7%), 5 mixed (8.8%), 2 incompatible (3.5%); preference, not performance
findings.rule: Liking peaks at moderate complexity, so Character should sit between floor and ceiling. Preference is not performance.
findings.engine: Character dial; kick and tick density
findings.verification_note: Western Sydney portal abstract confirms 50/57 = 87.7%, with 5 mixed and 2 incompatible. Note that it is a 'segmented' inverted U and a vote count.

findings.claim: Medium syncopation maximises wanting-to-move and pleasure (inverted U); complex harmony attenuates the rhythm effect on pleasure.
findings.sources: Witek, Clarke, Wallentin, Kringelbach & Vuust (2014). Syncopation, body-movement and pleasure in groove music. PLOS ONE 9(4):e94446. Matthews, Witek, Heggli, Penhune & Vuust (2019). PLOS ONE 14(1):e0204539. Also Stupacher, Wrede & Vuust (2022) PLOS ONE replication
findings.design: Online ratings. Witek: N=66 (57 in some analyses), 50 drum breaks at 120 bpm, syncopation index 0-81. Matthews: varied rhythm and harmony complexity.
findings.effect: Witek quadratic R²=.347 (move), .427 (pleasure). Matthews: inverted U for rhythm; high-complexity chords weakened rhythm's effect on pleasure; training strengthened the inverted U.
findings.rule: Medium syncopation maximises groove, i.e. motor engagement, which is plausibly an arousal and distraction risk for focus work (untested for performance). Lean low-syncopation for Deep, Read and Write.
findings.engine: Kick and tick placement (syncopation); swing; Energise; Character dial
findings.verification_note: Witek full text checked (N, 120 bpm, 0-81 index, R² .3474/.4267). Matthews abstract confirmed. The 2015 correction was not checked. The focus-performance implication is the researcher's inference, which I flagged.

findings.claim: Groove ratings for drum breaks peak at about 100-120 bpm across 60-200 bpm.
findings.sources: Etani, Marui, Kawase & Keller (2018). Optimal tempo for groove: its relation to directions of body movement and Japanese nori. Frontiers in Psychology 9:462. doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2018.00462
findings.design: Lab listening, 30 synthesized drum breaks (5 patterns x 6 tempi: 60, 75, 100, 120, 150, 200 bpm); N=35 analysed
findings.effect: Tempo F(2.83,96.25)=21.81, ηp²=0.391. Quadratic optimum 107-126 bpm per pattern; adjusted R² small (0.03-0.23).
findings.population: Japanese music majors (Tokyo University of the Arts), age 18-40
findings.rule: About 105-125 bpm is the band of maximal urge-to-move for drum breaks. Sitting slower suits Deep work if motor pull is to be avoided; the boundary is fuzzy (small R²).
findings.engine: Tempo per job; state change Energise
findings.verification_note: Full text checked. Added the effect size, the exact optimum estimate (107-126 bpm) and the population (music majors, N=35), which limits generality.

findings.claim: In a large drum-pattern corpus, syncopation and event density explain very little groove variance; listener style bias explains more. Residual microtiming and beat salience showed no effect.
findings.sources: Senn, Kilchenmann, Bechtold & Hoesl (2018). Groove in drum patterns as a function of both rhythmic properties and listeners' attitudes. PLOS ONE 13(6):e0199604
findings.design: Online, 248 patterns analysed, 665 participants analysed (929 recruited), 8,329 ratings analysed
findings.effect: Syncopation R²=0.010, event density R²=0.011, style bias R²=0.123, familiarity η²=0.051; microtiming and beat salience n.s. Exploratory.
findings.rule: Event density moves groove only slightly; listener style preference explains about ten times more variance, which argues for user taste control over fine pattern tuning.
findings.engine: Kick and tick density; Character dial; swing and humanise
findings.verification_note: Full text checked; all figures match. Authors call it exploratory and non-causal.

findings.claim: POPULAR CLAIM: microtiming ('feel', humanised offsets) makes rhythm groove or swing more. Quantised versions are rated as high or higher, and expanded deviations are rated lower.
findings.sources: Frühauf, Kopiez & Platz (2013). Music on the timing grid: the influence of microtiming on the perceived groove quality of a simple drum pattern performance. Musicae Scientiae 17(2):246-260. Datseris et al. (2019). Microtiming deviations and swing feel in jazz. Scientific Reports 9:19824 (arXiv 1904.03442)
findings.design: Online ratings. Frühauf: 93 music students, rock pattern, snare/bass shifts of -25, -15, 0, +15, +25 ms. Datseris: 160 listeners, 12 jazz piano recordings quantised, expanded or inverted.
findings.effect: Frühauf: quantised rated highest, ratings fell as deviation grew; early and snare shifts penalised more. Datseris: quantised slightly higher than original; expanded lower.
findings.rule: Default to quantised timing. Even ±15 ms systematic shifts were rated below quantised in Frühauf, so there is no evidence-based 'safe' offset; 'under 15 ms' is not established. No source here tests swing ratio, so do not claim swing ratio is 'the meaningful knob'.
findings.engine: Swing and humanise
findings.verification_note: Both abstracts confirmed. Corrected the rule: the 15 ms cap is not supported (±15 ms was already worse than 0 ms), and the swing-ratio claim has no source. Senn et al. 2016 found original microtiming rated equal to quantised, so the popular claim is unsupported rather than reversed.

findings.claim: Human rhythmic timing deviations are long-range correlated (1/f-type). Listeners preferred a song humanised with 1/f deviations over one humanised with white-noise deviations.
findings.sources: Hennig, Fleischmann, Fredebohm, Hagmayer, Nagler, Witt, Theis & Geisel (2011). The nature and perception of fluctuations in human musical rhythms. PLOS ONE 6(10):e26457
findings.design: Performance recordings (metronome reproduction by singing/drumming) plus a listening test with Göttingen choir singers on a pop song in 1/f vs white-noise humanised versions
findings.effect: 1/f version 'clearly preferred' and rated more precise. Exact percentage (64%), N and SD not verified (in images). Exponents vary widely across performers.
findings.rule: If humanising is used, draw offsets from a correlated (1/f) process, not independent jitter. The SD size is not established, and C3-15 suggests quantised may beat any humanising.
findings.engine: Swing and humanise
findings.verification_note: PLOS full text fetched; qualitative result confirmed, numeric details are in images. The 64% figure and the 'equal SD' design detail could not be confirmed. Removed the pairing with a '<15 ms cap', which C3-15 does not support.

findings.claim: In Jones et al. (2002), pitch judgments were most accurate for tones at the rhythmically expected time (inverted U around the expected onset); the effect vanished with irregular or absent interpolated rhythm.
findings.sources: Jones, Moynihan, MacKenzie & Puente (2002). Temporal aspects of stimulus-driven attending in dynamic arrays. Psychological Science 13(4):313-319. Large & Jones (1999). Psychological Review 106(1):119-159
findings.design: Lab pitch comparison with regular vs irregular interpolated tones (3 experiments)
findings.effect: Accuracy profile peaked at the expected onset; absent with irregular rhythm (no ES verified)
findings.rule: Do not assume a steady pulse improves attention to the user's (visual or cognitive) work. No number supported.
findings.engine: Kick and tick density (pulse regularity)
findings.verification_note: Psychological Science abstract confirms the content; the author list was not visible in the snippet. Large & Jones 1999 was not checked. Replication failure confirmed via C3-18.

findings.claim: Replications of the Jones et al. (2002) pitch-comparison paradigm failed: only 40 of 140 participants across five experiments (including an exact replication) showed the inverted-U profile, and group means never replicated. A separate N=181 study found no behavioural benefit of in-phase rhythmic cueing for pitch discrimination.
findings.sources: Bauer, Jaeger, Thorne, Bendixen & Debener (2015). The auditory dynamic attending theory revisited: a closer look at the pitch comparison task. Brain Research 1626:198-210. doi:10.1016/j.brainres.2015.04.032. Lin, Oetringer et al. (2022). No behavioural evidence for rhythmic facilitation of perceptual discrimination. European Journal of Neuroscience 55:3352-3364. doi:10.1111/ejn.15208
findings.design: Bauer: 5 lab experiments, N=140 total. Lin et al.: three task versions, N=181.
findings.effect: Bauer: 40/140 (29%) showed the effect; group-level null in every experiment. Lin: no accuracy or RT advantage for in-phase vs out-of-phase or random targets.
findings.rule: Behavioural benefit from rhythmic entrainment in pitch tasks is not established. Do not justify the beat on 'entrainment improves attention'. No number supported.
findings.engine: Kick and tick density
findings.verification_note: Both papers confirmed. Correction: '38 of 106 in another lab' is the same group's 2014 SysMus conference report of an earlier stage, not an independent replication. Lin et al. 2022 (Lin, Oetringer et al.) is a different Lin from C3-08. Grade raised to moderate because two well-powered nulls agree. Bauer suggests other paradigms may still support dynamic attending.

findings.claim: A 3 Hz frequency-modulated sound entrains delta-phase neural oscillations, and gap detection depends on the entrained phase (preferred phase varies by individual). This is neural entrainment within a narrow auditory task.
findings.sources: Henry & Obleser (2012). Frequency modulation entrains slow neural oscillations and optimizes human listening behavior. PNAS 109(49):20095-20100. doi:10.1073/pnas.1213390109. Haegens & Zion Golumbic (2018). Rhythmic facilitation of sensory processing: a critical review. Neurosci Biobehav Rev 86:150-165. doi:10.1016/j.neubiorev.2017.12.002
findings.design: EEG lab study; critical review
findings.effect: Detection clustered at preferred delta phases; delta phase predicted behaviour better than stimulus phase or ERP. Review flags inconsistent terminology and methodological caveats.
findings.rule: Entrainment affects perception of the sound itself, not demonstrably unrelated work. Do not claim cross-modal focus benefits.
findings.engine: Tempo per job (no rule beyond arousal)
findings.verification_note: Both citations and abstracts confirmed. Sample size and statistics for Henry & Obleser were not checked.

findings.claim: Binaural beats: one meta-analysis reports a medium pooled effect (g=0.45) on memory, attention, anxiety and pain, with pre-task exposure and longer exposure working better. A second meta-analysis/systematic review of 15 studies reports mixed results for attention and memory.
findings.sources: Garcia-Argibay, Santed & Reales (2019). Efficacy of binaural auditory beats in cognition, anxiety, and pain perception: a meta-analysis. Psychological Research 83(2):357-372. doi:10.1007/s00426-018-1066-8. Basu & Banerjee (2023). Potential of binaural beats intervention for improving memory and attention: insights from meta-analysis and systematic review. Psychological Research 87(4):951-963. doi:10.1007/s00426-022-01706-7
findings.design: Garcia-Argibay: 22 studies, 35 ES. Basu & Banerjee: 15 studies.
findings.effect: g=0.45 (Garcia-Argibay); masking with white/pink noise unnecessary; before or before-and-during exposure beats during-only; longer exposure better. Basu & Banerjee: 'mixed results'; their pooled g=0.40 and 31 ES not verified.
findings.rule: Evidence is mixed and the mechanism unsupported (C3-21), so do not build state changes on binaural beat frequency. If tested, it would be pre-task exposure, not a during-task bed.
findings.engine: State changes; beds
findings.verification_note: Garcia-Argibay confirmed (PubMed abstract, g=0.45, 22 studies, 35 ES). Basu & Banerjee: title, venue, DOI and 15 studies confirmed; the g=0.40 figure could not be verified, so I removed it from the confirmed effect.

findings.claim: POPULAR CLAIM: binaural beats entrain brainwaves to the beat frequency and shift arousal. A controlled EEG/physiology study found no band-power change and no HR or skin-conductance change. A systematic review found 5 of 14 studies consistent with entrainment, 8 contradictory and 1 mixed.
findings.sources: López-Caballero & Escera (2017). Binaural beat: a failure to enhance EEG power and emotional arousal. Frontiers in Human Neuroscience 11:557. doi:10.3389/fnhum.2017.00557. Ingendoh, Posny & Heine (2023). Binaural beats to entrain the brain? A systematic review. PLOS ONE 18(5):e0286023
findings.design: Lab EEG baseline-beat-post epochs (3 min) at theta, alpha, beta, gamma and upper gamma, binaural and acoustic; systematic review of 14 EEG studies
findings.effect: No matching-band EEG change, no HR or SC change (López-Caballero). 5/14 consistent, 8/14 contradictory, 1 mixed (Ingendoh).
findings.rule: Do not market or design 'theta for Settle, beta for Energise' binaural modes. Use tempo, density and level for arousal instead.
findings.engine: State changes (Settle -> Deep -> Energise)
findings.verification_note: Both confirmed. Corrected the design: López-Caballero tested theta through upper gamma, not delta. Ingendoh counts are confirmed; the Results section counts 6 supportive if the mixed one is included.

findings.claim: White/pink noise gives a small task-performance benefit in youth with ADHD or high symptoms and a small cost in non-ADHD groups.
findings.sources: Nigg, Bruton, Kozlowski, Johnstone & Karalunas (2024). Systematic review and meta-analysis: do white noise or pink noise help with task performance in youth with ADHD or ADHD symptoms? JAACAP 63(8):778-788. doi:10.1016/j.jaac.2023.12.014 (PMC11283987)
findings.design: Meta-analysis: ADHD k=13, N=335 (11 child, 2 college); non-ADHD k=11
findings.effect: ADHD g=+0.249 (95% CI .135-.363), I² <0.01. Non-ADHD g=-0.212 (CI -.355 to -.069) in abstract (-0.206 in Results). GRADE moderate. 12/13 white noise, 1 pink, 0 brown. dB levels variable and not pooled.
findings.population: Children and college-age, ADHD or high symptoms
findings.task: Lab attention and memory tasks, brief exposures
findings.rule: A noise bed may help attention-difficult listeners and hurt typical ones. Make the noise floor a per-user option, off by default. No dB level supported.
findings.engine: Beds (noise floor); Character dial; per-listener profile
findings.verification_note: PMC full text checked; all numbers match (minor abstract vs Results discrepancy for non-ADHD g noted). Pickens et al. 2019 not checked.

findings.claim: Moderate Brain Arousal model: white noise helped inattentive children's executive-function performance and harmed super-attentive children's non-EF (verbal memory) performance; no inverted U was found.
findings.sources: Söderlund, Sikström & Smart (2007). Listen to the noise. J Child Psychol Psychiatry 48(8):840-847. doi:10.1111/j.1469-7610.2007.01749.x. Helps, Bamford, Sonuga-Barke & Söderlund (2014). PLOS ONE 9(11):e112768. Baijot et al. (2016). Behav Brain Funct 12:11. doi:10.1186/s12993-016-0095-y
findings.design: Helps: N=90 children aged 8-10 (36 sub, 29 normal, 25 super-attentive), WN at 65/75/85 dB (EF) and 65/70/75 dB (non-EF). Baijot: 30 children aged 7-12 with/without ADHD, Go/Nogo. Söderlund 2007: ADHD vs controls, memory tasks.
findings.effect: Helps: sub-attentive EF improved F(2,66)=7.39, p=.001; super-attentive declined on non-EF tasks F(2,46)=4.42, p=.018 (EF decline n.s., F=.20). Little change moderate to high; no inverted U. Söderlund: noise helped ADHD, hurt controls. Baijot: noise reduced omissions in ADHD.
findings.rule: Benefit appeared at lab levels (about 70-75 dB) that are too loud for hours of listening, and no inverted U was found. The effective safe dose for adults over hours is unknown; cap well below lab levels.
findings.engine: Beds (noise floor level); Sensory Guard; per-listener profile
findings.verification_note: Helps PMC text checked. Corrected the age (8-10, not 7-14) and the super-attentive result (decline only on non-EF tasks; EF decline n.s.). Added that the authors 'failed to produce an inverted U-curve'. Baijot's 77 dB level and 13/17 split were not verified (abstract gives N=30, age 7-12). The replications are mostly from the same research group.

findings.claim: Beta-range (16 Hz) amplitude modulation added to music improved sustained attention over time more for high-ADHD-symptom listeners in one industry-run study. Modulation depth had no effect.
findings.sources: Woods, Hewett et al. (2024). Rapid modulation in music supports attention in listeners with attentional difficulties. Communications Biology 7. doi:10.1038/s42003-024-07026-3 (PMC11499863); Author Correction 2025 (PMC12420781). Woods is a Brain.fm employee with equity; Hewett was one at the time.
findings.design: Exp1 online SART N=83; Exp2 fMRI N=34; Exp3 EEG N=40; Exp4 online N=175 (rate analysis N=82, depth N=93); rates 8/16/32 Hz; depths low/med/high
findings.effect: Exp1 music x block ηp²=0.669 (F(38,38)); modulated music helped only when presented early. Exp4 rate x block x ASRS F(1,80)=4.03, p=.048, ηp²=0.048. Depth n.s. Results text contradicts itself on which ASRS group benefited.
findings.population: Online adults with self-reported ADHD symptoms
findings.rule: Possible ADHD-specific lever: 16 Hz AM on the bed. Evidence is marginal (p=.048), conflicted and industry-funded; do not adopt as a default.
findings.engine: Beds (modulation); per-listener profile
findings.verification_note: PMC full text checked: Ns, rates, stats, the depth null, conflicts of interest and the ASRS wording inconsistency all confirmed. Added the 2025 author correction (an author was added) and the rate-analysis N=82.

findings.claim: Introverts are more harmed by background music/noise than extraverts (Eysenck). Support is mixed: Küssner's review of 12 studies finds as much evidence for as against.
findings.sources: Furnham & Bradley (1997). Applied Cognitive Psychology 11:445-455. Cassidy & MacDonald (2007). The effect of background music and background noise on the task performance of introverts and extraverts. Psychology of Music 35(3):517-537. doi:10.1177/0305735607076444. Küssner (2017). Frontiers in Psychology 8:1991. doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2017.01991
findings.design: Lab studies N=20 (Furnham & Bradley), N=40 (Cassidy & MacDonald); narrative review of 12 studies
findings.effect: Küssner: 8 studies supportive in at least one task, 4 null in all; at task level 13 support vs 21 do not. Null-interaction studies: N=144, 92, 69, 58. Cassidy & MacDonald supported the theory on Stroop only, not on recall.
findings.rule: Personality-specific presets are not justified; let the user calibrate Character. The claim that low-arousal music is robustly less disruptive than high-arousal music or noise for everyone was not verified here.
findings.engine: Character dial; Settle default
findings.verification_note: Küssner full text checked. Corrected the null-study Ns (69, not 77). Cassidy & MacDonald supported the theory only on Stroop. The 'robust part' of the rule (low-arousal music less disruptive for everyone) is not shown by these sources as checked, so it was demoted. Furnham & Bradley details came from Küssner's table, not the original.

findings.claim: Music generally impaired complex task performance, complex music facilitated simple task performance, and preference for external stimulation (a dimension of boredom proneness) moderated these effects.
findings.sources: Gonzalez & Aiello (2019). More than meets the ear: investigating how music affects cognitive task performance. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied 25(3):431-444. doi:10.1037/xap0000202
findings.design: Lab experiment: silence vs music varying in complexity and volume, simple vs complex tasks (N not verified)
findings.effect: Direction as stated; ES not verified
findings.rule: Raise complexity for simple, monotonous jobs (Hours/Hold) and lower it for complex jobs (Write/Design/Read). Stimulation-seekers can take more. No number supported.
findings.engine: Character dial; kick and tick density per job
findings.verification_note: Abstract retrieved via Europe PMC and matches all three claims. The N of about 142 could not be verified, so I treat it as unknown.

findings.claim: Mehta et al. reported that moderate ambient noise (70 dB) beat both 50 dB and 85 dB on creative tasks in adults. A within-subject child study at about 64 dB(A) found no noise benefit.
findings.sources: Mehta, Zhu & Cheema (2012). Is noise always bad? Exploring the effects of ambient noise on creative cognition. Journal of Consumer Research 39(4):784-799. doi:10.1086/665048. Massonnié, Rogers, Mareschal & Kirkham (2019). Frontiers in Psychology 10:381. doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2019.00381
findings.design: Mehta: lab experiments, between-subjects (adults). Massonnié: within-subject, N=44 children aged 5-11, mean 64.3 dB(A) (range 52.8-76.1)
findings.effect: Adults: 70 > 50 and 85 dB (ES not verified). Children: AUT fluency noise effect F(1,38)=0.21, BF01=12.66.
findings.rule: For Design/ideation a moderate ambient level may help; 85 dB is clearly too loud. A 70 dB default is not established.
findings.engine: Sensory Guard (level ceiling); Design job level
findings.verification_note: Mehta existence confirmed via Crossref; its 70/50/85 result confirmed only through Massonnié's description. Massonnié checked: children, within-subject, about 64 dB rather than 70, so it is not a direct replication (the authors say Mehta may not replicate in children).

findings.claim: In isolated instrument sounds, a few acoustic features (ratio of high to low frequency energy, attack slope, spectral regularity) predict 50-57% of the variance in rated valence and energy arousal.
findings.sources: Eerola, Ferrer Flores & Alluri (2012). Timbre and affect dimensions: evidence from affect and similarity ratings and acoustic correlates of isolated instrument sounds. Music Perception 30(1):49-70. doi:10.1525/mp.2012.30.1.49
findings.design: Three lab experiments: ratings of 110 and 105 isolated instrument sounds (equal pitch, duration, dynamics) plus dissimilarity task; acoustic regression
findings.effect: 50-57% of valence and energy-arousal variance predicted by few features. Direction (brighter = more arousal) not stated in abstract. Tension arousal not included in that figure.
findings.rule: Brightness (high/low energy ratio) and attack are candidate arousal levers alongside tempo. Direction and size for sustained beds are not established; test by ear.
findings.engine: Character dial (brightness); kick and tick attack; state changes
findings.verification_note: Abstract retrieved via Crossref. Corrected: the 50-57% applies to valence and energy arousal, not tension arousal; the abstract does not state the direction 'brighter = higher arousal' (plausible but unverified).

findings.claim: Decreased sound tolerance (hyperacusis) is common in autism: current prevalence about 41%, lifetime about 61%.
findings.sources: Williams, Suzman & Woynaroski (2021). Prevalence of decreased sound tolerance (hyperacusis) in individuals with autism spectrum disorder: a meta-analysis. Ear & Hearing 42(5):1137-1150. doi:10.1097/AUD.0000000000001005. (Ben-Sasson et al. 2019 J Autism Dev Disord: not verified)
findings.design: Three-level Bayesian meta-analysis: 67 articles; interview/questionnaire k=103 estimates, n=13,093
findings.effect: Current 41.42% (95% CrI 37.23-45.84%), lifetime 60.58% (50.37-69.76%); objective/observational current 27.30% (14.92-46.31%; k=8, n=488). Heterogeneity substantial; prevalence rose with age in ADI-R studies. Mean sample age 7.88 y.
findings.rule: Roughly 3-4 in 10 autistic users may find typical levels or transients aversive. Keep level ceilings, soft attacks, no sudden onsets and slow fades. No dB threshold for music beds exists.
findings.engine: Sensory Guard; fades; change budget; kick and tick attack
findings.verification_note: Williams abstract retrieved via Europe PMC; all prevalence figures confirmed. The Ben-Sasson 2019 'large ES' half could not be verified (search budget exhausted, DOI lookup failed), so I removed it from the claim. Adjusted the rule to reflect the 27% objective estimate.

findings.claim: POPULAR CLAIM: listening to Mozart boosts spatial or cognitive ability. A meta-analysis finds small effects, inflated by publication bias and lab affiliation. What remains is explained by arousal and mood.
findings.sources: Pietschnig, Voracek & Formann (2010). Mozart effect-Shmozart effect: a meta-analysis. Intelligence 38(3):314-323. doi:10.1016/j.intell.2010.03.001. Supporting: Husain et al. (2002) (C3-03) reports many failed replications with the PF&C task
findings.design: Meta-analysis (study count and pooled ES not verified)
findings.effect: Not verified from source; reported as small effects, larger in originating lab, with publication bias
findings.rule: No genre or composition boosts cognition per se. Effects run through arousal and mood (C3-03), so tune arousal levers, not 'smart music' content.
findings.engine: Character dial; tempo per job
findings.verification_note: Existence, authors, venue and DOI confirmed via Crossref. The abstract and effect sizes could not be retrieved (ScienceDirect 403; search budget exhausted), so the effect field is marked unverified. The Husain 2002 discussion independently notes many failed PF&C replications and the arousal-mood account.

findings.claim: Background sound slightly impairs reading comprehension overall. Intelligible speech and lyrical music do the most harm. Instrumental music was judged by the authors not to affect comprehension. Effects are similar for children and adults, and reading speed is barely affected.
findings.sources: Vasilev, Kirkby & Angele (2018). Auditory distraction during reading: A Bayesian meta-analysis of a continuing controversy. Perspectives on Psychological Science 13(5):567-597. doi:10.1177/1745691617747398 (PMC6139986)
findings.design: Bayesian meta-analysis; 54 studies with comprehension outcomes and 13 with reading speed (the total of 65 was not confirmed)
findings.effect: Comprehension vs silence: all sounds g=-0.21 [-0.30,-0.13] (k=54); speech -0.26 [-0.36,-0.17] (k=20); music -0.19 [-0.34,-0.05] (k=36); noise -0.17 [-0.33,0.002] (k=12). Lyrical minus non-lyrical music: -0.19 (95% probability lyrical is worse). Intelligible minus unintelligible speech: -0.12 (99% probability). Reading speed: g=-0.06 [-0.15,0.02]. Children minus adults: -0.01 [-0.10,0.08]. The authors conclude that instrumental music while reading does not affect comprehension.
findings.population: Adults and children, mostly lab studies
findings.rule: For Read: no voice, no lyrics and no speech-like spectral detail. The meta-analysis's 'music' estimate (g≈-0.19) mixes lyrical and instrumental pieces, so it should not be read as the cost of an instrumental bed. The authors' conclusion is that instrumental music has roughly no effect, meaning the realistic best case is no help and no measurable harm. Noise is borderline (credible interval touches 0). No level or tempo number is supported.
findings.engine: Read job design: bed voicing (no vocal or formant-like timbres)
findings.verification_note: Opened the PMC full text. Table 2 values for all sounds, speech, music, noise and reading speed match exactly, and so does Table 3 (children vs adults). The lyrical vs non-lyrical contrast (-0.19, P≈.95) is right. Corrected: the intelligible vs unintelligible speech contrast is -0.12 at 99% probability. The pooled 'lyrical g≈-0.35', 'intelligible g≈-0.34' and 'non-lyrical vs noise P=.55' figures were not found in the parts I read, so I removed them. The rule overreached: it said an instrumental bed costs about g=0.2, but the -0.19 is the pooled figure for all music, and the authors explicitly conclude that instrumental music does not affect comprehension. I rewrote the rule to match.

findings.claim: Across all outcomes, background music versus no music averages to about a null effect, because specific effects cancel out. It reliably hurts reading, slightly hurts memory, and helps emotion and sport. Faster music tempo speeds up the tempo of behaviour.
findings.sources: Kämpfe, Sedlmeier & Renkewitz (2011). The impact of background music on adult listeners: A meta-analysis. Psychology of Music 39(4):424-448. doi:10.1177/0305735610376261
findings.design: Meta-analysis: 66 music-vs-no-music samples (n=4,501) and 71 music-vs-music samples (n=6,821)
findings.effect: Global music vs none: weighted r=.03. Reading: weighted r=-.11 (8 studies, n=680, range -.39 to -.02, all negative). Other memory tasks: weighted r=-.09 (8 studies, n=274). Loudness manipulations: r=.02 (9 studies, n=1,593). Tempo overall: r=-.01 (16 studies). Tempo of music on tempo of behaviour: weighted r=.40 (8 studies, range .13-.67).
findings.task: Mixed: reading, memory, sport, consumer behaviour, emotion
findings.rule: Do not promise a cognitive gain from the music itself, and make any claim task-specific. Tempo carries over to behavioural pace (r=.40), but the 8 studies behind that figure measured eating, shopping, driving and exercise, not typing or knowledge work. 'Keep tempo moderate for typing jobs' is therefore an extrapolation. No BPM number is supported.
findings.engine: Each job's design (per-task claims); kick/tick tempo per job
findings.verification_note: Downloaded the full PDF and extracted the text. Confirmed r=.03 global, 66 samples, n=4,501, reading r=-.11 (8 studies, n=680, all negative, -.39 to -.02), loudness r=.02 (9 studies), and tempo-on-behaviour r=.40 (8 studies). Added the memory figure, r=-.09. The 'cognition (achievement) r=-.01' figure is ambiguous in the extracted table (the unweighted mean is -.02). I corrected the rule because the tempo studies (Caldwell & Hibbert restaurant, Milliman supermarket, Roballey eating, and others) are not typing tasks.

findings.claim: (As stated by the researcher) Background music impairs learning overall, and music without lyrics is the least harmful. CORRECTED: this meta-analysis reports a small POSITIVE pooled effect of background music on learning (d=0.314), with classical music the most favourable genre.
findings.sources: de la Mora Velasco, Chen, Hirumi & Bai (2023). The impact of background music on learners: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Psychology of Music 51(6):1598-1626. doi:10.1177/03057356231153070
findings.design: Random-effects meta-analysis, 71 effect sizes from 47 studies (published up to 2021), including music played before the assessment
findings.effect: Pooled d=+0.314 in favour of background music. The effect was medium and positive when music was played before the learning assessment, and small and positive for factual knowledge retention and for classical music versus other genres. Age is a possible moderator.
findings.task: Learning outcomes (mixed designs, including music before assessment)
findings.rule: Do not cite this meta-analysis as evidence that music harms learning; it reports the opposite. Its pooled estimate mixes music during the task with music before it, so it says little about continuous background sound during Read or Write. It conflicts with Vasilev 2018 and Kämpfe 2011 for reading, and that conflict is unresolved. No engine number is supported.
findings.engine: Read/Write job design (no change justified by this source)
findings.verification_note: Retrieved the abstract through the Semantic Scholar API and confirmed the DOI and citation through Crossref. The abstract states five results, the first being a small positive mean effect (d=0.314) in favour of background music, and says the results refute cognitive-load theories that discourage background music. The researcher's claim that music impairs learning overall is the reverse of the source. The direction, claim, effect and grade have been rewritten. It could equally be logged as a rejection of the original claim.

findings.claim: Music with lyrics hurts verbal and visual recall. A lo-fi instrumental track had no credible effect on any task (verbal or visual recall, reading, arithmetic). Participants were aware that lyrics hurt them, but rated lo-fi as neutral or even beneficial.
findings.sources: Souza & Leal Barbosa (2023). Should we turn off the music? Music with lyrics interferes with cognitive tasks. Journal of Cognition 6(1):24. doi:10.5334/joc.273 (PMC10162369)
findings.design: Within-subjects online study, University of Porto psychology students, N=106-123 per task; no preregistration mentioned
findings.effect: Lyrics vs silence: verbal d=-.32 [-.51,-.13]; visual -.33 [-.52,-.15]; reading -.19 [-.37,.00]; arithmetic -.11 [-.31,.08]. Lo-fi vs silence: verbal -.16 [-.34,.03]; visual -.23 [-.41,-.04] (Bayesian evidence ambiguous); reading +.14 [-.05,.32]; arithmetic -.05 [-.24,.14]. The authors state that lo-fi effects were not credible in any task.
findings.task: Verbal and visual recall, reading comprehension, arithmetic
findings.rule: A lo-fi-style instrumental bed is close to neutral for reading and arithmetic, and possibly carries a small visual-memory cost (d≈-0.2, inconclusive). Never use lyrics. Users' sense that the music helps is not evidence that it does.
findings.engine: Each job's design (Read, Hold); the studies' next versions (measure, don't rely on self-report)
findings.verification_note: Opened the PMC full text and confirmed all d values and Ns. Corrected two points: (1) the authors classify the visual-memory lo-fi effect as ambiguous and say lo-fi effects were not credible in any task, so 'costs about d=0.2 on visual memory' was overstated; (2) participants are not identified by nationality, only as University of Porto students. The self-report finding is confirmed: lo-fi was rated beneficial after reading (mean 2.31 on a -10 to +10 scale).

findings.claim: Irrelevant-sound effect: background sound with spectral or pitch change between successive events disrupts serial short-term memory whatever its meaning. Overall playback level does not change the effect, and it does not habituate. Stationary noise and a repeated identical syllable have no effect. Speech produces by far the largest effect, and pure pitch or FM variation produces only small ones.
findings.sources: Ellermeier & Zimmer (2014). The psychoacoustics of the irrelevant sound effect. Acoustical Science and Technology 35(1):10-16. doi:10.1250/ast.35.10
findings.design: Narrative review plus a re-analysis of an unpublished FM-rate study (24 participants) and a noise-vocoded speech study (20 Japanese listeners)
findings.effect: Speech raises errors about 50% over silence (relative difference in error rate). The most harmful FM tone raises them 22.5%. Continuous FM peaks near 4 Hz with about an 11% decrement; for interrupted FM the peak is even lower. Noise-vocoded speech with 1-2 bands has no effect, while 4-20 bands almost double errors. Stationary noise and a repeated syllable have no effect, level does not matter, and there is no habituation. Spectral change is necessary and level change alone is not.
findings.rule: For memory and order-holding jobs: avoid speech-like spectrally rich changing sounds, which are the main threat. Pitch or FM movement alone costs much less (≤22.5% vs about 50% for speech), with continuous FM most disruptive near 4 Hz and interrupted pitch sequences at lower rates. Turning the volume down does not remove the effect, so the fix is structural. Expect no habituation. The '1-8 events per second' and 'ban 2-8 Hz' bands are not from the source; the only supported anchor is a peak near 4 Hz for continuous FM.
findings.engine: Melodic event rate per job; change budget; Sensory Guard
findings.verification_note: Downloaded the J-STAGE PDF and extracted the text. Confirmed: speech about 50%, worst FM 22.5%, continuous-FM maximum near 4 Hz at about 11%, 24 participants, stationary noise and repeated syllable null, level irrelevant, no habituation, spectral change necessary and level change insufficient, 4 Hz AM noise not maximal. Corrected the rule: the '1-8 per second' and '2-8 Hz' ranges are invented; the paper says interrupted FM peaks below 4 Hz; and the review stresses that maximal effects need rich spectral (speech-like) detail.

findings.claim: Fluctuation strength (a sensation that peaks at 4 Hz modulation) partly predicts how much a background sound disrupts serial recall, but it fails for some sound classes.
findings.sources: Schlittmeier, Weißgerber, Kerber, Fastl & Hellbrück (2012). Algorithmic modeling of the irrelevant sound effect (ISE) by the hearing sensation fluctuation strength. Attention, Perception, & Psychophysics 74(1):194-203. doi:10.3758/s13414-011-0230-7; critique in Ellermeier & Zimmer (2014) doi:10.1250/ast.35.10
findings.design: Model fitted to about 40 background sounds across 70 behavioural measurements
findings.effect: Predicted performance fell within the interquartile range in 63 of 70 cases. All real-world sounds were modelled adequately. It overestimated the disruption from synthetic steady-state sounds (a repeated vowel or tone). Ellermeier & Zimmer report 55% of variance explained, and argue it should mispredict 4 Hz AM noise (which is not maximally disruptive) and noise-vocoded speech.
findings.rule: Fluctuation strength is a usable offline audit metric for beds and ticks in memory-heavy jobs: keep it low. It does not separate AM from FM, and it overpredicts for synthetic repeated tones, so pair it with listening tests. No threshold value is supported.
findings.engine: Sensory Guard (offline audit metric)
findings.verification_note: Retrieved the abstract through Europe PMC and confirmed the citation through Crossref. Corrected the count from about 50 sounds to about 40 sounds and 70 measurements, and the 90% figure to 63/70. Added the abstract's own failure mode (synthetic steady-state sounds). The 55% variance and the AM-noise and vocoder critique come from the Ellermeier & Zimmer text, which I verified.

findings.claim: Both liked and disliked music impaired serial recall compared with quiet, and liked music impaired it more than disliked music. This fits the acoustic-variation (changing-state) account.
findings.sources: Perham & Sykora (2012). Disliked music can be better for performance than liked music. Applied Cognitive Psychology 26(4):550-555. doi:10.1002/acp.2826
findings.design: Lab, serial recall of 8-item lists in quiet, liked and disliked music conditions (N not verified)
findings.effect: Both music conditions were significantly worse than quiet, and liked music was significantly worse than disliked. Effect sizes were not retrieved.
findings.rule: Do not assume preference protects performance on memory-heavy work. No number is supported.
findings.engine: Character dial (preference is not a performance proxy)
findings.verification_note: Retrieved the abstract through OpenAlex and confirmed the citation through Crossref. The main result is confirmed. The abstract does not support the claim that listeners fail to notice the harm, so I removed that clause. The N of about 25 and the 'thrash metal' detail could not be verified.

findings.claim: Instrumental music disrupted reading comprehension only when it was both fast and loud (tempo x intensity interaction). The fast/loud condition fell below a silent baseline.
findings.sources: Thompson, Schellenberg & Letnic (2012). Fast and loud background music disrupts reading comprehension. Psychology of Music 40(6):700-708. doi:10.1177/0305735611400173
findings.design: Lab, repeated measures, N=25; silent baseline from separate control participants (pilot 2); tempo and intensity steps equated psychologically (pilot 1)
findings.effect: Significant tempo x intensity interaction, with fast/loud below baseline. The cell means (2.38/2.43/2.96/1.95 vs 2.77), the F value and the 110/150 bpm and 60/72.4 dB values could not be verified because the full text is paywalled.
findings.rule: For Read, avoid combining a high event rate with a high level. Exact bpm and dB anchors come from one piece and N=25 and are unverified, so treat '110 bpm / 60 dB' and '40 bpm ≈ 12 dB' as provisional, not as law.
findings.engine: Read job design: coupled tempo and level ceiling
findings.verification_note: Retrieved the abstract through OpenAlex; the publisher returned 403. The abstract confirms the design, N=25, the separate baseline, the psychologically equated manipulations and the fast/high result. Downgraded the grade from moderate to weak: one piece, small N, and a between-subjects baseline. The specific numbers are unverified.

findings.claim: Background music while word-processing essays affects writing. Writers with musical training and higher working-memory span wrote better essays.
findings.sources: Ransdell & Gilroy (2001). The effects of background music on word processed writing. Computers in Human Behavior 17(2):141-148. doi:10.1016/S0747-5632(00)00043-1
findings.design: Lab, undergraduates writing essays with and without music (N not verified)
findings.effect: A fluency drop with music was not verified (abstract unavailable). The verified summary says students with musical training and high working-memory span wrote better essays, with longer sentences and more pauses at clause boundaries.
findings.rule: Treat Write as a high-load verbal job, by extrapolation from reading. This paper alone cannot anchor a rule. No number is supported.
findings.engine: Write job design
findings.verification_note: The paper exists (Crossref). The abstract is elided on Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex, and only the Semantic Scholar TLDR was available, which mentions training and working-memory span but not a fluency drop. The headline claim is kept only as unverified.

findings.claim: In a 5-week field study, software developers' positive affect and self-rated work quality were lowest, and time-on-task longest, in the no-music week. A later 62-analyst study found music did not change data-modelling quality but did change mood.
findings.sources: Lesiuk (2005). The effect of music listening on work performance. Psychology of Music 33(2):173-191. doi:10.1177/0305735605050650; Lesiuk (2011). The effect of music listening, personality, and prior knowledge on mood and work performance of systems analysts. Int. J. Human Capital and IT Professionals. doi:10.4018/jhcitp.2011070105
findings.design: Field, 5 weeks, 56 developers in 4 Canadian firms; 2011: 62 systems analysts, 10 min of music
findings.effect: 2005: positive affect and quality lowest, and time-on-task longest, with no music (self-report). 2011: no effect of music on modelling quality, but effects on mood measures.
findings.rule: For programming, music's documented value is mood regulation. There is no controlled evidence that it improves code quality. No number is supported.
findings.engine: Design job design; Settle/Deep/Energise states
findings.verification_note: Both abstracts retrieved through OpenAlex. Confirmed 56 developers, 4 Canadian firms and 5 weeks. The 2005 abstract does not describe an ABAB design or call the correlations 'non-significant', so I dropped those details. Added the full citation for the 2011 paper. Changed replication from 'failed' to 'contested' because the 2011 study used a different design and outcome.

findings.claim: Moderate ambient noise (70 dB) improved creative-task performance compared with low noise (50 dB), and high noise (85 dB) hurt it. The proposed mechanism is processing difficulty leading to a higher construal level.
findings.sources: Mehta, Zhu & Cheema (2012). Is noise always bad? Exploring the effects of ambient noise on creative cognition. Journal of Consumer Research 39(4):784-799. doi:10.1086/665048
findings.design: 5 lab experiments
findings.effect: Inverted U across 50/70/85 dB. Effect sizes were not retrieved.
findings.task: Creative tasks; buying likelihood of innovative products
findings.rule: Weak support for a diffuse noise floor during ideation work. Do not transplant the 70 dB figure to hours of headphone listening. Treat it as a hypothesis.
findings.engine: Ideation job design: noise-texture layer
findings.verification_note: Retrieved the abstract through OpenAlex and confirmed the citation through Crossref. It confirms 5 experiments, 70 vs 50 vs 85 dB, and the construal mechanism. I could not check replications because the search budget was exhausted.

findings.claim: Background music with foreign lyrics, without lyrics, and with familiar lyrics all impaired compound remote associate (CRAT) performance compared with quiet. Positive mood and a habit of studying with music did not protect against this.
findings.sources: Threadgold, Marsh, McLatchie & Ball (2019). Background music stints creativity: Evidence from compound remote associate tasks. Applied Cognitive Psychology 33(5):873-888. doi:10.1002/acp.3532 (CC BY)
findings.design: 3 lab experiments (one music type per experiment) vs quiet
findings.effect: All music conditions significantly reduced CRAT solutions. Effect sizes and the library-noise result were not verified.
findings.rule: For convergent or insight phases, music is a cost. Offer a near-silent or steady mode. No number is supported.
findings.engine: Convergent-phase design: drop melodic and harmonic layers
findings.verification_note: Retrieved the abstract through Semantic Scholar and confirmed the citation through Crossref. The abstract confirms all three conditions and the mood and study-habit findings. The full text returned 403, so the library-noise comparison and effect sizes were not verified.

findings.claim: Happy (positive-valence, high-arousal) classical music raised overall divergent-thinking scores compared with silence. No condition affected convergent thinking (RAT).
findings.sources: Ritter & Ferguson (2017). Happy creativity: Listening to happy music facilitates divergent thinking. PLOS ONE 12(9):e0182210. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0182210
findings.design: Between-subjects, N=155 (149 analysed for alternative uses), 5 conditions
findings.effect: Overall divergent thinking: happy M=93.87 vs silence 76.10, t(57)=2.11, p=.039, d=.55. Fluency (p=.036) and originality (p=.017) did not survive the Bonferroni α≈.0083. RAT: F(4,150)=0.36, ηp²=.009.
findings.rule: Weak support for more energetic positive music during divergent generation and quiet during convergent work. No number is supported. The identity of the specific piece (Vivaldi) was not verified.
findings.engine: Divergent phase: Energise state
findings.verification_note: Opened the PLOS full text. All statistics match. The piece title (Table 1) was not visible, so 'Vivaldi Spring' remains unverified.

findings.claim: The Mozart effect is not specific to Mozart. Small spatial-task gains after music are explained by arousal and mood.
findings.sources: Pietschnig, Voracek & Formann (2010). Mozart effect-Shmozart effect: A meta-analysis. Intelligence 38(3):314-323. doi:10.1016/j.intell.2010.03.001; Thompson, Schellenberg & Husain (2001). Arousal, mood, and the Mozart effect. Psychological Science 12(3):248-251. doi:10.1111/1467-9280.00345
findings.design: Meta-analysis; lab experiment (Mozart vs Albinoni vs silence)
findings.effect: Thompson 2001 (verified): the Mozart advantage over silence disappeared when arousal, mood and enjoyment were held constant statistically. Pietschnig figures (d=0.37 Mozart vs control, 0.38 other music vs control, 0.15 Mozart vs other music, publication bias) were not verified; the abstract is inaccessible.
findings.rule: Do not claim any composer, genre or frequency makes users smarter. Tune arousal to the job.
findings.engine: Settle/Deep/Energise states (arousal route)
findings.verification_note: Both DOIs confirmed through Crossref. Retrieved the Thompson 2001 abstract through OpenAlex, which confirms the arousal and mood explanation. The Pietschnig abstract is elided everywhere I could reach, so its d values are marked unverified. The conclusion stands on Thompson 2001.

findings.claim: 16 Hz amplitude modulation in Brain.fm music was associated with better sustained attention, mainly for listeners with higher self-reported ADHD symptoms and early in the session. The evidence is a marginal interaction.
findings.sources: Woods, Sampaio, James, Przysinda, Cordovez, Hewett, Spencer, Morillon & Loui (2024). Rapid modulation in music supports attention in listeners with attentional difficulties. Communications Biology 7:1376. doi:10.1038/s42003-024-07026-3 (PMC11499863)
findings.design: 4 experiments: online SART N=83, fMRI N=34, EEG N=40, online N=175 (rate n=82, depth n=93). No preregistration mentioned. One author is a Brain.fm employee with equity, and another was an employee when the work was done.
findings.effect: Exp 1: music x order F(10,150)=2.30, p=.015, ηp²=.13 (benefit when AM music came first). Exp 4: rate x block x ASRS F(1,80)=4.03, p=.048, ηp²=.048, with a quadratic peak at 16 Hz. Depth: no significant effects. About 48% exclusions in Exp 1.
findings.rule: 16 Hz AM at medium depth was the best of 8/16/32 Hz (16 Hz equals 32nd notes at 120 bpm). The evidence is marginal and conflicted, so it can be an opt-in texture at most and never a default or a claim.
findings.engine: Opt-in AM layer; Sensory Guard
findings.verification_note: Opened the PMC full text. All statistics and the conflict-of-interest details match. Added the missing author (Cordovez, confirmed via Crossref) and the high exclusion rate. Exp 1 compared AM music with slow-modulated music and pink noise.

findings.claim: In an Arctop and Endel-funded at-home EEG study, Endel's soundscape raised EEG-decoded focus over silence on average, while Spotify and Apple playlists did not. But among under-36s all three audio conditions beat silence.
findings.sources: Haruvi, Kopito, Brande-Eilat, Kalev, Kay & Furman (2022). Measuring and modeling the effect of audio on human focus in everyday environments using brain-computer interface technology. Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience 15:760561. doi:10.3389/fncom.2021.760561
findings.design: Within-subjects at home, 62 recruited and 51 analysed, 4 one-hour sessions, Muse-S EEG, per-person random forest (r=0.6 with self-report). All authors from Arctop. Funded by Arctop and Endel; Endel was involved in study design and supplied the stimuli.
findings.effect: rmANOVA F(3,150)=4.28, p=.006. Endel vs silence ΔM=0.090, p=.008 (Holm). Apple p=.11, Spotify p=.65. Working subgroup (n=26): Endel > silence. Under-36 (n=25): Endel p=.004, Apple p=.001, Spotify p=.005, all better than silence. Over-36 and non-working: no differences.
findings.rule: Use only as motivation to test. The under-36 result shows playlists working as well as Endel, so 'generative beats playlists' is not supported. No number is supported.
findings.engine: The studies' next versions (behavioural outcomes vs silence and vs playlists)
findings.verification_note: Opened the Frontiers full text. The main statistics and conflicts match. Corrected the researcher's 'effect only in under-36s': in that subgroup all three conditions beat silence, which undercuts the Endel-specific claim. The '7x' marketing figure was not checked.

findings.claim: Preferred background music raised the share of time on task during a 30-minute low-demand vigilance task, by reducing mind-wandering. It did not reduce external distraction or improve reaction time.
