list: Attention lasts about 10 minutes (or 8 seconds), so stimulation must change on that cadence. Bradbury 2016 finds no primary evidence; the figure spread through repeated citation.
A waking 90-minute BRAC justifies 90-minute focus cycles. The REM cycle is sleep-dependent (Moses et al. 1977), and waking ultradian rhythms are weak and contested.

People get used to distracting background sound. Bell et al. 2019 (N = 273, preregistered) found no habituation of changing-state or deviant effects within or across sessions; Banbury & Berry 2005 office workers reported none.
Novelty or rarity is what captures attention. Vachon et al. 2012 and Parmentier 2014 show capture comes from violated predictions, not novelty or rarity as such.
Brief periodic 'mental breaks' or cues prevent the vigilance decrement. Helton & Russell 2012 (N = 498) found no benefit, with Bayesian evidence for the null.
Background music generally boosts performance. Kämpfe et al. 2011 found a null overall effect, with reading and memory slightly impaired.
Sounds become more liked simply through repeated exposure. Montoya et al. 2017 found the exposure-liking inverted U for visual but not auditory stimuli.
The looming bias for rising sounds is an evolved adaptive bias. Kolarik et al. 2026 (Hearing Research) show a loudness model predicts the asymmetry without one.

Search-budget note: the session's web-search limit was exhausted after the first query. All checks were done by fetching DOIs and publisher, Crossref, Europe PMC and PMC records directly, so counter-literature I could not fetch is flagged as unverified in the notes.

'Nature sounds such as water and birds are inherently better focus backgrounds than engineered noise': Hongisto et al. (2017), in a 15-week office field study, found no water sound better than pseudo-random noise. Babbling water and bird calls were worse. Comfort tracked spectral steadiness, not naturalness.

'Turn the volume down and distraction goes away': Ellermeier & Hellbrück (1998) found the same serial-recall disruption at 60 and 75 dB(A). What mattered was the changing sound's prominence over a steady masking floor.

'Rising sounds are always perceived as changing more (a universal looming bias)': Olsen & Stevens (2010, Perception 39:695) found the bias at high intensities but reversed at low intensities, which is the region a background engine works in.
'Crossfeed reduces headphone listening fatigue': this is a practitioner assertion (bs2b) with no controlled study. The externalisation review (Best et al. 2020) does not cover crossfeed.

'Predictable, regular patterns grab attention because the brain detects them': Southwell et al. (2017) found that regularity does not capture attention. Random distractors were more disruptive, even though regular sequences evoke larger sustained EEG responses.

'A specific fade-in time such as 200 ms or more prevents attentional capture': rise-time numbers come from startle at 105 dB in humans or from dolphins (Götz 2020: 141 ms in one animal, over 220 ms in another). No study gives a rise time for low-level orienting.

'Changes are equally noticeable whether something appears or disappears': disappearance is far harder to detect in dense scenes (Cervantes Constantino et al. 2012). But 'appearances are always detected' is also an overstatement: it fails when the onset's loudness cue is masked.

'dB(A) is a sufficient comfort metric': unpleasantness is not predicted by A-weighted level (Ellermeier et al.). Loudness, sharpness and roughness carry it, and A-weighting underweights low-frequency annoyance (Persson Waye 2002).
'Low pure tones are the most annoying tonal components': in Yonemura et al. (2021) the tonal penalty was larger at 100-400 Hz than at 40-50 Hz.

Note: my web-search budget ran out partway through. Later checks used direct fetches of PMC, Crossref and Europe PMC records. Darwin & Ciocca 1992, the Fastl & Zwicker textbook values, the 2004 Acta Acustica Ellermeier paper and Blumenthal 1988's abstract could not be opened.

Binaural beats entrain brainwaves to the beat frequency ('theta for calm, beta for focus'): a controlled EEG study (López-Caballero & Escera 2017) found no band-power, HR or skin-conductance change, and a 2023 systematic review found only 5 of 14 EEG studies consistent with entrainment (8 contradictory).

The Mozart effect (classical music makes you smarter): Husain et al. 2002 shows the spatial gain follows tempo- and mode-driven arousal and mood; Nantais & Schellenberg's 'Schubert effect' (a preferred story works too) and many failed PF&C replications show no Mozart-specific effect.
60 bpm music slows your heart to match it: Koelsch & Jäncke 2015 found no studies showing heart-rate entrainment to musical beats; tempo acts only through general arousal, and effects are small.

Humanised or 'loose' microtiming makes beats groove more: quantised versions were rated highest (Frühauf 2013) or slightly higher than originals (Datseris 2019); expanded deviations reduce swing ratings; Senn 2018 found no effect of residual microtiming.

A steady rhythmic pulse sharpens attention through dynamic attending or entrainment: the Jones 2002 pitch-comparison result failed group-level replication in five experiments (Bauer 2015; 40/140 individuals), and a N=181 study found no behavioural benefit of rhythmic cueing (Lin, Oetringer et al. 2022). Any entrainment effect shown is within the auditory stream, not for unrelated visual or cognitive work.

The Yerkes-Dodson law shows an arousal-performance inverted U: the 1908 study was about stimulus (shock) strength and habit formation in mice; the arousal/stress version is a later reinterpretation often misattributed to the original (Teigen 1994).

White, pink or brown noise helps everyone focus: the meta-analytic benefit (g about 0.25) is in ADHD or high-symptom youth; non-ADHD groups show a small cost (g about -0.21); there are no brown-noise studies at all and only one pink-noise study (Nigg et al. 2024).

Noise effects follow a neat inverted U in children (Moderate Brain Arousal): Helps et al. 2014 explicitly failed to find an inverted U in any group, and lab doses (65-85 dB) exceed safe all-day listening.
Introverts need quieter or no music and extraverts need busier music: Küssner 2017 finds as much evidence against as for (13 supportive vs 21 non-supportive task results across 12 studies).
Moderate (70 dB) ambient noise boosts creativity, the 'coffee-shop effect': rests on one adult study (Mehta et al. 2012); a within-subject child study near 64 dB found no benefit (BF01 about 12.7).

Faster music always speeds you up or sharpens processing: Lin, Kuo & Mai 2023 found 138 bpm gave no gain over silence; only very slow (66 bpm) music slowed responses, and it also raised accuracy on the verbal task.

Note on verification limits: the shared web-search budget ran out mid-review. Teigen, Gonzalez & Aiello, Eerola, Williams, Mehta and Pietschnig were checked only by DOI lookup (Crossref or Europe PMC abstracts). Ben-Sasson 2019, Pietschnig's effect sizes, Basu & Banerjee's g=0.40, Hennig's 64% figure, Baijot's 77 dB level and Kiss 2024's exact statistics could not be verified.

'Background music helps learning' and 'background music harms learning' are both oversold. The de la Mora Velasco 2023 meta-analysis actually reports a positive pooled d=0.31 (mixing pre-task and during-task music), while the reading meta-analyses (Vasilev 2018, Kämpfe 2011) show small harms. The direction depends on the design.
Mozart effect: any gain is explained by arousal and mood (Thompson et al. 2001), not by Mozart.
'Brown noise helps ADHD focus': there are no trials. Nigg 2024 found no brown-noise studies, and white or pink noise slightly hurts people without ADHD.
'Endel beats playlists': in Haruvi 2022's under-36 subgroup, Spotify and Apple playlists also beat silence. The study is industry-funded, and its outcome is EEG-decoded focus.
'Turning music down removes distraction': the irrelevant-sound effect is independent of playback level (Ellermeier & Zimmer 2014).
'You get used to it': the irrelevant-sound effect does not habituate across trials or sessions.

'Music you like helps you concentrate': liked music impaired serial recall more than disliked music (Perham & Sykora 2012). Lo-fi was rated helpful after the fact, but its effects were not credible (Souza & Barbosa 2023).
'Water or nature masking beats noise': office field data show water-based masking was rated no better and often worse than pseudo-random noise (2017 Frontiers in Psychology field study).
'Introverts need silence': the personality x music interaction failed to replicate (Avila, Furnham & McClelland 2012).

gaps: No study gives a safe rate of gradual change (dB per minute, semitones per minute, or density change per minute) below which drift in a continuous background goes unnoticed. Slow-change deafness (C1-08) gives only one size (3 semitones) and its ramp duration was not retrieved.
No direct evidence on the optimal tide period, or on whether a periodic slow modulation (minutes-long) is better than an aperiodic (1/f) one for staying unnoticed over hours.

Habituation time constants for continuous non-speech music beds are unknown. The 20-minute figure comes from speech and office noise in one lab study, a field study found no habituation, and the large recent study (C1-03) found none for changing-state or deviant sound.

Whether variation across sessions (new seed each day vs the same figures) helps or hurts is untested. Implicit pattern memory persists for 7 weeks (C1-16), but its effect on boredom or distraction over days is not studied.
Studies measure disruption in minutes-long lab blocks. Almost nothing tests background sound over 2-4 hour real work sessions, where vigilance decrement, boredom and fatigue interact.

Mere-exposure and satiation research mostly uses short excerpts and attentive rating. Mere-exposure was null for auditory stimuli in the meta-analysis. How liking and boredom evolve for a generative bed heard incidentally for hours is unknown.

IDyOM-style information content and entropy have been linked to liking under attentive listening, but not to distraction or task performance under background listening. No IC or entropy target for 'unnoticed but not boring' exists.

No study identifies an optimal pattern vocabulary size (number of distinct figures or tokens) for background music. The token-set-size effects in the irrelevant-sound literature (Tremblay & Jones 1998, JEP:LMC 24:659) could not be read beyond the title.
How fade length affects capture for complex musical elements (not pure tones) is not quantified. The rising/falling asymmetry has no agreed ratio for designing fade-in vs fade-out times.

Individual differences relevant to the jobs (ADHD, autism, high vs low working-memory capacity) in habituation rate to changing background sound are largely unstudied, beyond the finding that WMC moderates deviant but not changing-state effects.
Whether background music prevents or slows the vigilance decrement over time on task (a music x time interaction) has not been established. Kiss & Linnell entered time on task only as a covariate.
The exposure duration for statistical learning of tone sequences (Saffran 1999) and how many minutes of exposure make a transition rule predictable were not verified.

No study measures rise time or fade-in length against attentional capture at low, background listening levels (about 40-65 dB). Startle and looming data come from loud stimuli (80-105 dB) or animals, so there is no evidence-based fade-in time for a quiet element entering a bed.
No study gives a level-rise rate or range (dB per second) below which a rising element stops triggering the rising-intensity warning or orienting response.

Grouping cues (onset synchrony, harmonicity, comodulation) are measured with brief lab tones. How they transfer to multi-minute musical beds, and how much mistuning or detune a sustained voice tolerates before it splits off over hours, is not known.

There is no evidence on how many concurrent layers a bed can hold before an entry becomes invisible. Disappearances get harder to detect with scene size, but appearances stay at ceiling up to 14 components.

There are no controlled studies of listening fatigue from hours of low-level headphone listening. Crossfeed's claimed fatigue benefit is untested, and no study links stereo width or in-head localisation to fatigue or to cognitive performance.

No validated sharpness or roughness ceiling exists for comfort over hours of music. The 1.75 acum annoyance-model threshold is a convention, and the unpleasantness studies used short clips of environmental sounds.
The low-frequency annoyance and cortisol findings come from loudspeaker ventilation noise at 40 dBA. Whether bass-heavy music beds on headphones have the same cost is untested.
Tonal-penalty data come from environmental noise. There is no evidence on whether sustained musical drones or pure tones in a deliberate tonal bed carry the same annoyance penalty.
Salience models reach only about AUC 0.74 on natural scenes. No validated salience model exists for music-like beds that a Sensory Guard could use with known accuracy.

Interactions are unstudied: whether shared modulation, onset synchrony and spatial placement add up to keep an element in the background, or whether one strong deviant cue (such as brightness) overrides the others.

Whether spatial separation of bed layers (panning) helps or hurts long-term comfort and focus is not addressed. Lateralising irrelevant speech gave only a partial benefit, and the effect on non-speech elements is unknown.

No study gives an optimal tempo, event rate (events/min) or kick/tick density for sustained cognitive work over hours. Tempo studies use 60-165 BPM excerpts for minutes, not generative beds for 1-4 h.
Inverted-U evidence for syncopation and groove is about pleasure and urge-to-move, not task performance. Whether moderate groove helps or hurts focus is untested.
No dose-response for loudness of a focus bed in typical adults: lab levels (65-85 dB) are above safe all-day listening, and the effective safe level is unknown.
White/pink noise ADHD benefit rests on brief child lab tasks (12/13 white noise). Effects in adults, over hours, with brown noise, or as a layer under music are unknown.

No validated way to place an individual on the arousal-optimum curve (introversion and ADHD as proxies are weak or contested). Real-time physiological targeting (HR, pupil, EDA) for a background-sound engine is untested.

Rhythmic entrainment benefits to cross-modal or cognitive attention (vs auditory perception) are unreplicated. Whether a steady pulse helps focus at all, compared with an arrhythmic bed, is unanswered.

Humanise: 1/f timing is preferred over random timing, but the SD size, the exponent across tempi, and whether any humanise beats quantised for background listening are unknown. Swing ratio effects on arousal are untested.

State transitions (Settle -> Deep -> Energise): no evidence on how fast tempo, density or brightness can change without causing an orienting response, or on the time course of arousal change after a change (Bernardi's pause effect is the only clue).
Brightness/timbre-arousal links come from isolated tones and ratings. There is no performance or physiology data for sustained beds or numeric spectral-centroid targets.
Autistic users: prevalence of sound intolerance is known, but no thresholds (dB, onset slope, transient rate) for tolerable music or noise beds exist; adult data are sparse.
Habituation: whether arousal effects of tempo or density persist or habituate over hours of listening (Bernardi saw no habituation within minutes) is unknown.
Binaural beats: no well-powered, preregistered, blinded trial during real work; meta-analytic g of about 0.4 is likely inflated by small studies.

No controlled study tests background sound during programming (writing or reading code, debugging). Programming evidence is limited to Lesiuk's self-report field work, so the Design and code jobs rest on extrapolation from reading and serial-memory findings.

No study tests sound during cross-domain idea combination (conceptual combination, analogy, the Fuse work). Ideation evidence covers only alternative-uses (divergent) and remote associates (convergent), with conflicting single studies (Mehta 2012, Ritter & Ferguson 2017, Threadgold 2019) and no meta-analysis of music or noise on creativity.

Maths: evidence is thin and mostly null for instrumental music (Souza & Barbosa d≈-0.05). Office noise hurts mental arithmetic (Banbury & Berry 1998), but no dose-response for event rate or level exists.

Nearly all task studies run 4-30 minutes. None test performance or fatigue over 2-8 hour sessions, so the Hours job and the change budget lack duration data. The ISE does not habituate across sessions, but music-specific long-session effects are unmeasured.

No study varies generative-music parameters (event rate in events/min, loop period, change rate, harmonic density) against task performance. Thompson et al. 2012 (tempo x level) is the nearest, with one piece and N=25.

Repetition fatigue in background (not focal) listening is not quantified. There is no data on how many minutes or repeats of a loop before users notice or tire, and game-audio sources are qualitative.
Mehta's 70 dB creativity effect has no independent preregistered replication, and its transfer to low-level headphone listening is untested.

The Endel and Brain.fm evidence is industry-funded with conflicted authors, uses EEG-decoded or symptom-subgroup outcomes, and lacks independent behavioural replication. No study compares a generative focus engine against a well-chosen instrumental playlist on objective work output.

Whether letting users choose (preference or control) offsets the cognitive cost of background sound is unresolved: Perham & Sykora say liked music is worse for memory, while Kiss & Linnell say preferred music improves task focus on low-load tasks.
Interactions with neurotype (ADHD, autism, introversion) are known only coarsely (noise g=+0.25 vs -0.21). There are no guidelines for profiling users or for safe adaptive switching between profiles.
The de la Mora Velasco et al. 2023 pooled effect and moderators (lyrics, tempo, volume) could not be verified because the paper is paywalled.
